intros.author: Jewish and Christian tradition ascribes the Pentateuch (Genesis–Deuteronomy) to Moses, and Jesus and the apostles refer to "the law of Moses" (e.g., Luke 24:44). Many modern critical scholars instead see the Pentateuch as compiled from several sources or traditions (the classic "JEDP" Documentary Hypothesis, now often replaced by supplementary or fragmentary models) and finalized during or after the Babylonian exile. Many conservative scholars hold to essential Mosaic authorship while allowing later editorial touches (e.g., updated place names such as "Dan" in 14:14, or the notice of Moses' death in Deuteronomy 34).
intros.date: If Mosaic, written c. 1446–1406 BC (early Exodus date) or the 13th century BC (late date). Critical scholarship generally places its final form in the 6th–5th centuries BC. The events narrated run from creation to the death of Joseph; the patriarchal period is often placed very roughly c. 2100–1700 BC, though dating is debated.
intros.audience: In the traditional view, Israel in the wilderness after the Exodus, learning who their God is and where they came from before entering Canaan. In critical views, Israel in or after exile reflecting on its identity and on God's promises.
intros.genre: Narrative prose with genealogies ("these are the generations of…", the toledot formula that structures the book), poetry (e.g., 49), and covenant texts. How literally to read chapters 1–11 is debated among Christians; Lutheran confessional teaching affirms them as true history given by God.
intros.purpose: To tell the beginnings of the world, of humanity, of sin and death, and of God's chosen family, and to show God's faithful promise carried forward through Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph despite human failure.
intros.themes: Creation by God's word; the fall into sin; judgment and grace (flood, Babel); covenant and promise (land, seed, blessing to all nations); election; God's providence ("ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good," 50:20).
outline: 25–28 Isaac and the struggle of Jacob and Esau
37–50 Joseph and Israel's descent into Egypt
intros.christ: Genesis 3:15, the promise that the woman's seed would crush the serpent's head, has been called the "first Gospel" (protoevangelium). The promise to Abraham that in his seed all nations would be blessed is applied to Christ by Paul (Gal 3:8, 16). Abraham's faith counted as righteousness (15:6) is the key text for justification by faith (Rom 4). Isaac's near-sacrifice (22), Melchizedek (14; Heb 7), and the scepter of Judah (49:10) have been read as pointing to Christ.
intros.empires: No world empire dominates the story. Egypt (Middle Kingdom and Second Intermediate period) is the great power to the south; Mesopotamian city-states and kingdoms (Sumerian, Akkadian, Amorite/Old Babylonian) lie to the east. Canaan is a patchwork of small city-states. The "kings of the east" in Genesis 14 have not been securely identified.
debated: Authorship — Traditional: Moses wrote the Pentateuch, with minor later updates. Critical alternative: compiled from earlier sources/traditions and completed in or after the exile.

Genesis 1–11 — Traditional/confessional: true history told in God's own words. Other readings: theological narrative using ancient Near Eastern literary forms, not intended as a scientific chronology; Christians differ on the age of the earth and the length of the creation days.

Patriarchal historicity — Traditional: real persons of the early 2nd millennium BC. Many critical scholars: later traditions with uncertain historical core (e.g., camels and Philistines are argued to be anachronisms; others answer that these reflect updating or early presence).
intros.setting: The ancient Near East of the Middle Bronze Age: city-states of Mesopotamia (Ur, Haran), Amorite migrations, the Old and Middle Kingdoms of Egypt, and Canaanite city-states. Genesis 1–11 shares themes with Mesopotamian literature (e.g., flood stories such as Atrahasis and the Gilgamesh epic), but presents one sovereign Creator rather than quarrelling gods. Customs in the patriarchal stories (adoption, inheritance, covenants, bride-price) have parallels in second-millennium texts such as those from Nuzi and Mari, though how closely they match is debated. Eden (linked to the Tigris and Euphrates), Mesopotamia (Ur of the Chaldees, Haran), Canaan (Shechem, Bethel, Hebron, Beersheba), the Negev, and Egypt (Goshen in the Nile Delta).

intros.author: Traditionally Moses (cf. 17:14; 24:4; 34:27, where Moses is told to write). Critical scholarship sees multiple sources and a final form in the exilic or post-exilic period.
intros.date: Traditional composition c. 1446–1406 BC or 13th century BC. The date of the Exodus itself is debated: the "early date" (c. 1446 BC) is based on 1 Kings 6:1 (480 years before Solomon's 4th year); the "late date" (c. 1270–1250 BC) is based partly on the city name Raamses (1:11) and archaeological arguments. Some scholars doubt a large-scale exodus altogether.
intros.audience: Israel as the newly redeemed covenant people of God.
intros.genre: Narrative, law (the Ten Commandments and the Book of the Covenant, 20–23), poetry (the Song of Moses, 15), and detailed instructions for the tabernacle.
intros.purpose: To record God's deliverance of Israel from slavery, the making of the covenant at Sinai, and the provision of the tabernacle so that the holy God might dwell among His people.
intros.themes: Redemption ("I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt," 20:2); the divine name (3:14); Passover; the Law given to a people already redeemed; God's presence; worship; intercession (Moses, 32–34); God's mercy and justice (34:6–7).
outline: 35–40 Tabernacle built and filled with glory
intros.christ: Christ is "our passover … sacrificed for us" (1 Cor 5:7); the Passover lamb, unblemished and with no bone broken (12:46; John 19:36), points to Him. The manna points to the true bread from heaven (John 6), the tabernacle to the Word who "dwelt" (literally "tabernacled") among us (John 1:14), and the Law drives sinners to Christ, its fulfillment.
intros.empires: New Kingdom Egypt (18th–19th Dynasties), then the leading power of the Near East, controlling Canaan through vassal city-states. Hittites to the north and Mitanni in Mesopotamia were rival powers in the same era.
debated: Date of the Exodus — Early date c. 1446 BC (1 Kings 6:1) vs. late date c. 1260 BC (city of Raamses, settlement archaeology).

Historicity and scale — Traditional: a real exodus of a large population (600,000 men, 12:37). Critical alternatives: a smaller group, a literary/theological memory, or no exodus at all; some evangelical scholars read the large numbers differently (e.g., "eleph" as clan or military unit).
Route and location of the sea and Mount Sinai remain uncertain.
intros.setting: Egypt of the New Kingdom (c. 1550–1070 BC), a powerful empire using forced labor on building projects. The Pharaohs of the oppression and exodus are not named in the text; candidates include Thutmose III / Amenhotep II (early date) or Seti I / Ramesses II (late date). The covenant at Sinai has a structure some scholars compare to ancient Near Eastern treaties (especially Hittite suzerainty treaties of the 2nd millennium BC). The Nile Delta (Goshen, Pithom, Raamses), the "Red Sea" (Hebrew yam suph, "sea of reeds"; exact location debated), the wilderness of Sinai, and Mount Sinai/Horeb (traditionally Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula, though other sites are proposed).

intros.author: Traditionally Moses; the book repeatedly says "the LORD spake unto Moses." Critical scholars assign most of it to the "Priestly" source (P) and the "Holiness Code" (17–26), dated variously from the pre-exilic to post-exilic periods.
intros.date: Traditional: during the year at Sinai, c. 1445 BC (early date) or 13th century BC. Critical: 7th–5th centuries BC for the final form, though much ritual material may be older.
intros.audience: The priests (sons of Aaron) and the whole congregation of Israel.
intros.genre: Ritual and legal instruction with brief narrative (8–10, 24).
intros.purpose: To teach Israel how a sinful people may live in the presence of a holy God: through sacrifice, priesthood, purity, and holy living.
intros.themes: Holiness ("ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy," 11:44; 19:2); atonement through blood (17:11); clean and unclean; the Day of Atonement (16); love of neighbor (19:18); sabbath and jubilee (25).
intros.christ: Hebrews 9–10 interprets the sacrifices and the Day of Atonement as shadows fulfilled once for all in Christ, who is both High Priest and sacrifice. The scapegoat bearing Israel's sins (16:21–22) pictures Christ bearing ours.
intros.empires: Egypt is the power Israel has just left; Canaan, under loose Egyptian control, lies ahead. No empire is active in the book itself.
debated: Date of the Priestly material — Traditional: Mosaic, at Sinai. Critical: priestly writing of the late monarchy, exile, or Persian period (with some scholars, e.g. in Jewish scholarship, arguing for pre-exilic origin of P).
Relationship of the "Holiness Code" (17–26) to the rest of the book.
intros.setting: Set at Mount Sinai in the month after the tabernacle was erected (Exod 40:17; Num 1:1). Sacrificial systems were common in the ancient Near East, but Leviticus distinctively ties sacrifice and purity to the holiness of the one God who dwells among His people. Mount Sinai and the camp of Israel around the tabernacle.

intros.author: Traditionally Moses (33:2 notes that Moses wrote down the journeys). Critical scholars see a composite of priestly and other sources.
intros.date: Traditional: end of the wilderness period, c. 1406 BC (early date) or 13th century BC. The narrative covers about 38 years.
intros.audience: The new generation of Israel about to enter Canaan.
intros.genre: Narrative, census lists, law, itineraries, and poetic oracles (Balaam).
intros.purpose: To show how the generation that came out of Egypt perished in the wilderness through unbelief, while God remained faithful and brought a new generation to the edge of the promised land.
intros.themes: Unbelief and its consequences (13–14); God's patience and judgment; holiness of the camp; leadership and rebellion (Korah, 16); God's blessing that cannot be cursed (22–24); the Aaronic benediction (6:24–26).
outline: 1–10 Preparation at Sinai: census and ordering of the camp
10–14 Journey to Kadesh and the failure to enter
26–36 The new generation prepared for the land
intros.christ: Jesus applies the bronze serpent lifted up in the wilderness (21:8–9) to His own crucifixion (John 3:14–15). Balaam's "Star out of Jacob" (24:17) was read messianically. Paul uses the wilderness events as warnings and points to Christ as the Rock (1 Cor 10:4).
intros.empires: Egypt in the background; the small kingdoms of Edom, Moab and Ammon, the Amorite kingdoms of Sihon and Og, and the Midianites are the powers Israel actually meets.
debated: Authorship and date — Traditional: Moses, in the wilderness period. Main critical view: compiled from several sources and completed in or after the exile (see Genesis).

The census numbers (603,550 fighting men, 1:46) — Traditional: literal totals. Alternatives: "thousand" (eleph) may mean a clan or troop, yielding much smaller numbers; others see symbolic or later figures.
intros.setting: The wilderness period after Sinai. Neighboring peoples include Edom, Moab, Ammon and the Amorite kingdoms of Sihon and Og east of the Jordan. An 8th-century BC inscription from Deir Alla (Jordan) mentions a seer "Balaam son of Beor," the same name as in Numbers 22–24, showing that traditions about such a figure circulated in the region. Sinai, the wilderness of Paran, Kadesh-barnea, the regions of Edom and Moab, and the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho.

intros.author: Traditionally Moses, whose speeches it records (1:1); the account of his death (34) is generally attributed to a later hand (Jewish tradition suggests Joshua). Many critical scholars connect the core of the book with the "book of the law" found in the temple under Josiah in 622 BC (2 Kings 22) and date it to the 7th century BC, with later additions.
intros.date: Traditional: c. 1406 BC (early date) or 13th century BC, on the plains of Moab. Critical: 7th century BC core, revised during the exile.
intros.audience: The second generation of Israel, about to enter Canaan.
intros.genre: Covenant sermons/speeches of Moses, law, poetry (the Song of Moses, 32; the Blessing of Moses, 33), and brief narrative.
intros.purpose: To renew the covenant with the new generation, calling them to love and obey the LORD in the land.
intros.themes: The Shema ("Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD," 6:4–5); covenant love and loyalty; remembering God's deeds; one place of worship; blessings and curses (28); choosing life (30:19); a prophet like Moses (18:15).
outline: 1–4 First address: history from Horeb to Moab
5–11 Second address: the great commandment and Ten Commandments
31–34 Succession of Joshua, Song and Blessing of Moses, death of Moses
intros.christ: Jesus answered Satan's temptations with Deuteronomy (Matt 4:4, 7, 10; Deut 8:3; 6:16; 6:13). The promised prophet like Moses (18:15–19) is identified with Jesus (Acts 3:22). Paul cites "Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree" (21:23) of Christ, who became a curse for us (Gal 3:13).
intros.empires: Egypt (remembered as the "house of bondage") and the small Transjordanian kingdoms. If the book's core belongs to Josiah's era (critical view), the Neo-Assyrian Empire, whose vassal treaties it resembles, is the background.
debated: Authorship and date — Traditional: Moses' speeches on the plains of Moab, c. 1406 BC or 13th century BC. Critical: a 7th-century BC work connected with Josiah's reform, extended during the exile.
Treaty form — Similarities to 2nd-millennium Hittite treaties (supporting an early date) vs. to 7th-century Assyrian treaties (supporting a late date); both are argued.
intros.setting: Israel camped in Moab after the defeat of Sihon and Og. The book's structure resembles ancient Near Eastern covenant treaties (preamble, history, stipulations, blessings and curses, witnesses); scholars debate whether it matches 2nd-millennium Hittite treaties or 7th-century Assyrian treaties more closely. The plains of Moab, east of the Jordan opposite Jericho; Mount Nebo (Pisgah), from which Moses viewed the land.

intros.author: Anonymous. Jewish tradition (Talmud, Baba Bathra 14b) credits Joshua with most of the book, with the account of his death added by others (Eleazar and Phinehas). The text notes Joshua wrote certain words "in the book of the law of God" (24:26) and repeatedly says things remain "unto this day," which suggests some distance from the events.
intros.date: Events c. 1406–1380 BC (early Exodus date) or c. 1230–1200 BC (late date). Traditional view: written soon after the events. Many critical scholars treat Joshua as part of a "Deuteronomistic History" (Deuteronomy–2 Kings) compiled in the 7th–6th centuries BC from older material.
intros.audience: Israel settling in the land, called to remember that the land was God's gift and to remain faithful to the covenant.
intros.setting: Canaan at the end of the Late Bronze Age: fortified city-states ruled by local kings, many nominally subject to Egypt. Israel crosses the Jordan opposite Jericho and campaigns in the central hill country, the south (Shephelah) and the north (Hazor).
intros.empires: Egypt's control of Canaan was weakening (the 14th-century Amarna letters show Canaanite kings pleading with Pharaoh against raiders called Habiru). No empire intervenes in the book; Canaanite city-state kings and their coalitions are Israel's opponents.
intros.genre: Historical narrative, with long lists of territorial boundaries and cities (13–21) and covenant speeches (23–24).
intros.purpose: To show that the LORD kept His promise to give Abraham's descendants the land, and to call Israel to wholehearted faithfulness.
intros.themes: God's faithfulness to His promises (21:45); holy war and the judgment of the Canaanites' sin (cf. Gen 15:16); courage grounded in God's presence (1:9); obedience and disobedience (Achan, 7); the inheritance; covenant choice ("as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD," 24:15).
outline: 1–5 Preparation and crossing of the Jordan
13–21 Division of the land; cities of refuge and Levitical cities
23–24 Joshua's farewell and covenant renewal at Shechem
intros.christ: "Joshua" (Yehoshua, "the LORD saves") is the Hebrew form of the name Jesus; Hebrews 4:8 contrasts the rest Joshua gave with the greater rest Christ gives. Rahab, saved by faith and the scarlet cord, appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:5) and among the heroes of faith (Heb 11:31). The "captain of the host of the LORD" (5:13–15), who receives worship, has often been understood as the pre-incarnate Son.
debated: Date of the conquest — tied to the early (c. 1406 BC) or late (13th century BC) Exodus date.

Archaeology — Traditional: a rapid initial campaign (Jericho, Ai, Hazor) followed by gradual occupation (13:1; Judg 1). Critical alternatives: peaceful infiltration, or a social revolt within Canaan; the evidence at Jericho and Ai is disputed, while a 13th-century destruction of Hazor is well attested.
Ethics of the herem ("utterly destroy") commands and how literally the summary statements ("all the land," 11:23) are to be read alongside reports of remaining Canaanites.

intros.author: Anonymous. Jewish tradition (Baba Bathra 14b) assigns it to Samuel. The refrain "In those days there was no king in Israel" (17:6; 21:25) suggests writing in the early monarchy. Critical scholars see it as part of the Deuteronomistic History, edited in the 7th–6th centuries BC.
intros.date: Covers roughly the period between Joshua and Samuel: c. 1380–1050 BC (early date) or c. 1200–1050 BC (late date). Many of the judges were probably regional and overlapping, so the years cannot simply be added up.
intros.audience: Israel in the early monarchy (traditional view) or in the late monarchy and exile (critical view), learning why apostasy brings ruin.
intros.setting: The hill country of Canaan in the early Iron Age. Israel is a loose tribal confederation without central government, surrounded and oppressed by neighbors.
intros.empires: No great empire; Egypt was in decline after c. 1150 BC. The pressures are local: Moab, Ammon, Midianites and Amalekites, Canaanite kings of Hazor, and above all the Philistines, one of the "Sea Peoples," who settled on the southern coast c. 1175 BC and possessed iron-working skill.
intros.genre: Historical narrative arranged in a repeated cycle, with poetry (the Song of Deborah, 5, one of the oldest poems in the Bible).
intros.purpose: To show the downward spiral of Israel's unfaithfulness and the repeated mercy of God who raised up deliverers, and to prepare for the need of a faithful king.
intros.themes: The cycle of sin, oppression, crying out, and deliverance (2:11–19); God's patience; the Spirit of the LORD empowering weak deliverers; moral and religious chaos when "every man did that which was right in his own eyes."
outline: 1:1–3:6 Incomplete conquest and the pattern of apostasy
3:7–16:31 The judges: Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar, Deborah and Barak, Gideon, Abimelech, Tola, Jair, Jephthah, Ibzan, Elon, Abdon, Samson
17–21 Appendices: Micah's idol and Dan's migration; the outrage at Gibeah and civil war with Benjamin
intros.christ: Each judge is a flawed and temporary savior; together they show Israel's need for the perfect Deliverer. Samson, whose greatest victory came in his death (16:30), faintly foreshadows Christ's victory through death, though Samson's sins are plainly reported. Hebrews 11:32 lists several judges among those who acted by faith.
debated: Chronology — the total of years given (over 400) vs. 1 Kings 6:1's 480 years from Exodus to Solomon; most solutions assume overlapping judgeships.
Date and editing of the book (early monarchy vs. Deuteronomistic editing in the 7th–6th centuries BC).
The relationship between Judges 1 (gradual, partial conquest) and Joshua's summaries.

intros.author: Anonymous. Jewish tradition (Baba Bathra 14b) names Samuel, though the genealogy ending with David (4:17–22) implies writing at least during David's reign.
intros.date: The story is set "in the days when the judges ruled" (1:1), roughly the 12th–11th centuries BC. Composition: traditionally the early monarchy (10th century BC); many critical scholars propose a post-exilic date (5th century BC), sometimes reading it as a protest against the ban on foreign wives in Ezra–Nehemiah. Others argue on linguistic grounds for a pre-exilic date.
intros.audience: Israel, especially readers interested in the ancestry of David.
intros.setting: Bethlehem in Judah and the land of Moab across the Dead Sea, during a famine in the period of the judges.
intros.empires: None. Moab, Israel's often hostile neighbor east of the Dead Sea, is the foreign land involved (cf. Deut 23:3).
intros.genre: Short historical narrative, carefully crafted, ending with a genealogy.
intros.purpose: To show God's hidden providence and loving-kindness (hesed) in preserving a family line that leads to King David, and to show a foreign woman embraced by the God of Israel.
intros.themes: Hesed (covenant loyalty and kindness); providence in ordinary events; the kinsman-redeemer (go'el); the inclusion of a Gentile ("thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God," 1:16); emptiness turned to fullness.
outline: 4 Boaz redeems; birth of Obed; genealogy to David
intros.christ: Boaz, the kinsman-redeemer who willingly pays the price to redeem and takes a foreign bride, is a picture of Christ our Redeemer and the Church His bride. Ruth the Moabitess appears in Christ's genealogy (Matt 1:5), a sign that the Gentiles belong in the promise.
debated: Date of composition — Traditional: early monarchy (the genealogy ends with David, not Solomon). Main critical view: post-exilic, sometimes read as a response to the mixed-marriage reforms of Ezra–Nehemiah.
Purpose — primarily a story of providence leading to David (traditional), or also a polemic against post-exilic exclusivism (some critical scholars).

intros.author: Anonymous. 1 Chronicles 29:29 mentions records of "Samuel the seer," "Nathan the prophet," and "Gad the seer"; Jewish tradition credits Samuel with chapters 1–24 and Nathan and Gad with the rest. 1 and 2 Samuel were one book in the Hebrew Bible; the Septuagint and Vulgate called them 1–2 Kingdoms / 1–2 Kings (hence older references to "I Kings" for 1 Samuel). Critical scholars see Samuel as part of the Deuteronomistic History, using older sources such as an "Ark Narrative" and the "History of David's Rise."
intros.date: Events c. 1100–1010 BC. Composition: traditionally after the division of the kingdom (note "kings of Judah," 27:6), using contemporary records; critical scholars propose final editing in the 7th–6th centuries BC.
intros.audience: Israel reflecting on the origins of the monarchy and of David's dynasty.
intros.setting: The transition from the judges to the monarchy: Shiloh's sanctuary, the Philistine wars, Saul's reign from Gibeah, and David's years as a fugitive in the Judean wilderness and among the Philistines.
intros.empires: No great empire; Egypt and Assyria were both weak at this time, which allowed a kingdom to rise in Israel. The Philistines, with their five cities (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath) and iron monopoly (13:19–22), are the main power.
intros.genre: Historical narrative, with poetry (Hannah's song, 2:1–10).
intros.purpose: To show how God established kingship in Israel, rejecting proud Saul and choosing David, "a man after his own heart."
intros.themes: God raises the humble and brings down the proud (2:7–8); obedience is better than sacrifice (15:22); God looks on the heart (16:7); the LORD as Israel's true king; the anointed one (Hebrew mashiach, "messiah"); faithful friendship (David and Jonathan).
outline: 1–7 Samuel: birth, call, the ark captured and returned
8–15 Saul: Israel demands a king; Saul's rise and rejection
16–31 David and Saul: David anointed, Goliath, flight, Saul's death on Mount Gilboa
intros.christ: Hannah's song ends with the LORD exalting "the horn of his anointed" (2:10), echoed in Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55). David, the shepherd-king anointed in Bethlehem, chosen though despised, prefigures Jesus, the Son of David, born in Bethlehem.
debated: Sources and date — near-contemporary records (traditional) vs. late compilation from older sources (critical).

Apparent doublets (e.g., two accounts of David's introduction to Saul, 16 and 17; two occasions of sparing Saul, 24 and 26) — explained as separate events or complementary accounts (traditional) or as merged sources (critical).

Historicity of David's kingdom — some minimalist scholars doubted it; the 9th-century "House of David" inscription from Tel Dan has made his existence widely accepted, though the size of his kingdom is still debated.

intros.author: Anonymous (see 1 Samuel). Prophetic records of Nathan and Gad are likely sources (1 Chr 29:29).
intros.date: Events of David's reign, c. 1010–970 BC. Composition as with 1 Samuel.
intros.audience: Israel, learning the meaning of God's covenant with David and the consequences of sin even in a chosen king.
intros.setting: David's reign, first at Hebron over Judah (7½ years), then at Jerusalem over all Israel (33 years). Jerusalem, captured from the Jebusites, becomes the political and religious capital.
intros.empires: A power vacuum in the region (Egypt weak; Assyria not yet expanding west) allowed David to defeat the Philistines, Moab, Edom, Ammon, and the Aramean (Syrian) kingdoms such as Zobah and Damascus, building a modest regional empire.
intros.genre: Historical narrative (including the so-called "Succession Narrative," 9–20), poetry (David's lament for Saul and Jonathan, 1; David's psalm, 22, parallel to Psalm 18).
intros.purpose: To record David's reign and especially the Davidic covenant (7), while honestly displaying David's sins and their fruit in his family.
intros.themes: The Davidic covenant: an eternal house, kingdom and throne (7:12–16); sin, confession and forgiveness ("I have sinned against the LORD... The LORD also hath put away thy sin," 12:13); consequences of sin; God's faithfulness despite human failure.
outline: 1–4 David king over Judah; civil war
5–10 David king over all Israel: Jerusalem, the ark, the covenant, victories
13–20 Troubles in David's house: Amnon, Absalom's revolt, Sheba's revolt
21–24 Appendices: famine, warriors, David's song and last words, the census and the altar on Araunah's threshing floor
intros.christ: The promise of 2 Samuel 7 — that David's offspring would reign forever and be God's son — is fulfilled in Jesus, to whom "the Lord God shall give... the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32–33; Heb 1:5). David's confession and forgiveness (12; Ps 51) shows the Gospel of forgiveness for the penitent.
debated: Composition — the Succession Narrative as an early, near-eyewitness source (widely held) vs. later composition.

The census in 24:1 ("the LORD... moved David") compared with 1 Chronicles 21:1 ("Satan... provoked David"): understood as God permitting Satan's work in judgment (traditional harmonization) or as theological development (critical).

intros.author: Anonymous. Jewish tradition (Baba Bathra 15a) names Jeremiah. The book cites sources: "the book of the acts of Solomon" (11:41) and the "chronicles of the kings" of Israel and of Judah. 1 and 2 Kings were originally one book (called 3–4 Kingdoms in the Septuagint and 3–4 Kings in the Vulgate).
intros.date: Events c. 970–853 BC. Since 2 Kings ends with the release of King Jehoiachin in Babylon (562 BC), the whole work was completed during the exile, c. 560–540 BC. Critical scholars often posit a first edition under Josiah (late 7th century) and an exilic second edition.
intros.audience: The exiles in Babylon, asking why Jerusalem fell and whether God's promises still stood.
intros.setting: Solomon's reign and temple in Jerusalem; the division of the kingdom (c. 931/930 BC) into Israel (north, capital eventually Samaria) and Judah (south, capital Jerusalem); the ministry of Elijah during the reign of Ahab and Jezebel.
intros.empires: Egypt (Pharaoh Shishak/Shoshenq I invaded Judah c. 925 BC, 14:25; his own inscription at Karnak lists towns in Israel and Judah), Phoenicia (Hiram of Tyre, Solomon's ally; Jezebel was a Sidonian princess who promoted Baal worship), Aram-Damascus (Ben-hadad), and the rising Neo-Assyrian Empire (Ahab fought Shalmaneser III at Qarqar in 853 BC, known from Assyrian records though not mentioned in the Bible).
intros.genre: Historical narrative arranged by reigns, with synchronized chronology, prophetic narratives, and theological evaluation of each king.
intros.purpose: To show that Israel's and Judah's history was governed by their faithfulness or unfaithfulness to the covenant, particularly in worship, and that God's word through the prophets always comes to pass.
intros.themes: Wisdom and its loss (Solomon); the temple as the place of God's name; idolatry as the root sin ("the sins of Jeroboam"); the power of the prophetic word (Elijah on Carmel, 18); the still small voice (19:12); God preserving a remnant (19:18).
outline: 1–11 Solomon: accession, wisdom, temple, glory and apostasy
12–16 The divided kingdom: Rehoboam and Jeroboam to Omri
17–22 Elijah and Ahab; Micaiah; deaths of Ahab
intros.christ: Jesus is "greater than Solomon" (Matt 12:42) and the true temple (John 2:19–21). Elijah raising the widow's son (17) and the bread for the widow of Zarephath (Luke 4:25–26) foreshadow Christ's mercy to the Gentiles; the coming of "Elijah" is fulfilled in John the Baptist (Matt 11:14).
debated: Chronology of the kings — the reign totals do not add up simply; co-regencies and different reckoning systems (proposed especially by E. R. Thiele) are widely used to reconcile them.
Solomon's wealth and building — traditional acceptance vs. claims of exaggeration; archaeological interpretation of 10th-century remains (e.g., the gates at Hazor, Megiddo, Gezer) is contested.

Date and composition — Traditional: compiled from royal and prophetic records by a prophetic author during the exile (Jewish tradition named Jeremiah). Main critical view: part of a "Deuteronomistic History" (Joshua–Kings) edited in one or more stages, under Josiah and/or in the exile.

intros.author: Anonymous (see 1 Kings); traditionally Jeremiah.
intros.date: Events c. 853–561 BC. Completed after 562 BC (25:27–30), during the exile.
intros.audience: The Judean exiles in Babylon.
intros.setting: The ministry of Elisha; the decline and fall of the Northern Kingdom of Israel to Assyria (722 BC); Judah under good and bad kings (Hezekiah, Manasseh, Josiah); the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon (586 BC).
intros.empires: Aram-Damascus (Hazael, Ben-hadad); the Neo-Assyrian Empire (Tiglath-pileser III, Shalmaneser V, Sargon II, Sennacherib — whose siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC is also recorded in his own annals, which claim he shut Hezekiah up "like a bird in a cage" but do not claim the city's capture); Egypt (Pharaoh Necho killed Josiah at Megiddo in 609 BC); the Neo-Babylonian Empire (Nebuchadnezzar II, deportations of 605, 597 and 586 BC).
intros.genre: Historical narrative with prophetic stories and theological commentary (e.g., the sermon on the fall of Samaria, 17:7–23).
intros.purpose: To explain that the exile was God's just judgment for persistent idolatry despite many prophetic warnings, while keeping hope alive through the survival of David's line.
intros.themes: The prophetic word fulfilled; judgment on covenant-breaking (17; 24:3–4); reform and revival (Hezekiah, Josiah); the rediscovered book of the law (22); God's grace to a Gentile (Naaman, 5); hope for David's house (25:27–30).
outline: 9–17 Jehu's revolt to the fall of Samaria (722 BC)
18–25 Judah alone: Hezekiah, Manasseh, Josiah, the last kings and the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC); Jehoiachin released
intros.christ: Elisha's miracles — feeding a hundred men with a few loaves (4:42–44), raising the dead, healing a Gentile leper — foreshadow Jesus' works (Luke 4:27). The thread of hope for David's line in exile (25:27–30) leads to the Son of David.
debated: Chronology of the late kings (several synchronisms are hard to reconcile).

The account of Sennacherib's withdrawal (19:35) — a miraculous deliverance (traditional) vs. legendary development of an Assyrian withdrawal for other reasons; Assyrian records confirm the siege but not its end.
Date and editing, as with 1 Kings.

intros.author: Anonymous; "the Chronicler." Jewish tradition (Baba Bathra 15a) credits Ezra. Some scholars see the same hand in Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah (note the overlap of 2 Chr 36:22–23 with Ezra 1:1–3); many now think they are separate works.
intros.date: Written after the exile; the genealogies extend several generations beyond Zerubbabel (3:19–24), pointing to c. 450–400 BC (some propose the 4th century BC).
intros.audience: The post-exilic community in Judah, small and under Persian rule, needing to know they were still the people of God, connected to Israel's past and to David's line and temple.
intros.setting: Retells history from Adam to David (1 Chronicles) and from Solomon to the exile (2 Chronicles), using Samuel–Kings and other sources (it cites many prophetic and royal records).
intros.empires: Written under the Persian Empire. The history recounted touches Philistines, Arameans, and other neighbors of David's time.
intros.genre: Genealogies (1–9) followed by historical narrative with a strong focus on worship, temple, and Levites; a theological re-telling rather than a duplicate of Kings.
intros.purpose: To encourage the restored community by showing God's covenant with David and the central place of the temple and true worship in Israel's identity.
intros.themes: All Israel; David's line; the temple and its worship (music, Levites, priests); seeking the LORD; God's faithfulness across generations.
outline: 1–9 Genealogies from Adam to the returned exiles
11–21 David's reign: Jerusalem, the ark, the covenant, wars, the census
22–29 David's preparations for the temple; organization of priests, Levites, musicians; Solomon made king
intros.christ: The genealogies trace the line of promise from Adam through Judah and David, which Matthew and Luke continue to Jesus. God's promise to David to establish his son's throne "for ever" (17:11–14) is fulfilled in Christ.
debated: Authorship — Ezra/same author as Ezra–Nehemiah (traditional and some modern scholars) vs. separate author (many modern scholars).

Historical reliability of material unique to Chronicles (e.g., large numbers, Manasseh's repentance in 2 Chr 33) — accepted as drawn from authentic sources (traditional) vs. regarded as theological shaping (critical).

intros.author: The Chronicler (see 1 Chronicles); traditionally Ezra.
intros.date: c. 450–400 BC (see 1 Chronicles).
intros.audience: The post-exilic community under Persian rule.
intros.setting: From Solomon's reign and temple through the kings of Judah (the northern kingdom is mostly omitted except where it touches Judah) to the exile, ending with Cyrus' decree permitting the return (36:22–23).
intros.empires: Egypt (Shishak), Aram, Assyria (Sennacherib's invasion, 32), Babylon (Nebuchadnezzar), and finally Persia (Cyrus the Great, 539 BC).
intros.genre: Historical narrative with emphasis on worship, reform, prayer, and divine retribution.
intros.purpose: To show that faithfulness to the LORD and His temple brings blessing and unfaithfulness brings ruin, and that repentance is always possible, so that the restored community would seek the LORD.
intros.themes: "If my people... shall humble themselves, and pray... then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin" (7:14); temple-centered reform (Hezekiah, Josiah); immediate retribution and grace for the penitent (Manasseh, 33:12–13); God's sovereignty over kings and empires.
outline: 10–36 Kings of Judah from Rehoboam to Zedekiah; reforms of Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah; fall of Jerusalem; Cyrus' decree
intros.christ: The temple filled with glory (5:13–14; 7:1) points to Christ, the true temple in whom God dwells with His people (John 1:14; 2:21). The Hebrew Bible ends with 2 Chronicles' summons, "Who is there among you... let him go up" (36:23), looking forward to restoration fulfilled in Christ.
debated: See 1 Chronicles (authorship; reliability of unique material).
Manasseh's repentance (33:10–20), absent from Kings — accepted as historical (traditional) or regarded as the Chronicler's theology (critical).

intros.author: Traditionally Ezra, "a ready scribe in the law of Moses" (7:6); chapters 7–10 include first-person memoirs of Ezra. Ezra and Nehemiah were one book in the Hebrew Bible. Many scholars suppose a later compiler (sometimes equated with the Chronicler).
intros.date: Events 538–c. 458 BC (with a gap of nearly 60 years between chapters 6 and 7). Composition c. 440–400 BC. Parts are in Aramaic, the official language of the Persian Empire (4:8–6:18; 7:12–26), including copies of Persian official documents.
intros.audience: The returned exiles in Judah (the Persian province of Yehud).
intros.setting: The return from Babylon under Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel (538 BC), the rebuilding of the temple (completed 516/515 BC) despite opposition, and Ezra's later mission (458 BC, under Artaxerxes I) to teach the law.
intros.empires: The Persian (Achaemenid) Empire: Cyrus the Great (whose policy of allowing deported peoples to return and restore their sanctuaries is also reflected in the "Cyrus Cylinder"), Darius I, Xerxes I (Ahasuerus), Artaxerxes I. Judah is a small province within the satrapy "Beyond the River."
intros.genre: Historical narrative with lists, official letters, and first-person memoir.
intros.purpose: To show God's faithfulness in restoring His people and temple as promised through the prophets (1:1; Jer 29:10), and to call the community to live by God's law.
intros.themes: God moving the hearts of kings (1:1; 7:27); rebuilding worship; the Word of God read and taught (7:10); opposition; purity of the covenant people; confession of sin (9).
outline: 3–6 Rebuilding the altar and temple; opposition; completion and Passover
9–10 The problem of mixed marriages; confession and reform
intros.christ: The restored temple and people were the setting for the Messiah's coming; the faithfulness of God in bringing back a remnant preserved the line of David (Zerubbabel appears in Jesus' genealogy, Matt 1:12–13). Ezra's priestly confession and intercession (9) foreshadow Christ's intercession for His people.
debated: Order of Ezra and Nehemiah — traditional: Ezra came in 458 BC (7th year of Artaxerxes I), before Nehemiah (445 BC). Alternative: Ezra came under Artaxerxes II in 398 BC, after Nehemiah; a "middle" view emends the date to 428 BC.

The dissolution of mixed marriages (10) — interpreted as a necessary safeguard against idolatry (cf. Deut 7:3–4; Neh 13:26) or criticized as excessive; Ruth and Jonah are sometimes read as counterpoints.

intros.author: Largely the first-person memoir of Nehemiah (1:1), incorporated with other material (lists, Ezra's reading of the law) by a compiler; traditionally Ezra or Nehemiah himself.
intros.date: Events 445–c. 430 BC (Nehemiah's first term began in the 20th year of Artaxerxes I; he later returned for a second term, 13:6). Composition c. 430–400 BC.
intros.audience: The Jewish community in Jerusalem and Judah under Persian rule.
intros.setting: Nehemiah, cupbearer to Artaxerxes I at Susa, is appointed governor and returns to rebuild Jerusalem's walls, completed in 52 days despite opposition from Sanballat (governor of Samaria), Tobiah the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arab. Sanballat and Geshem are attested in extra-biblical sources (the Elephantine papyri and an inscription, respectively).
intros.empires: The Persian Empire under Artaxerxes I Longimanus (465–424 BC); Jerusalem is a minor provincial town within it.
intros.genre: Memoir and historical narrative, with lists of names, a covenant document, and prayers.
intros.purpose: To record the restoration of Jerusalem's walls and the community's covenant renewal, and to show the need for continual reform.
intros.themes: Prayer joined to action (1:4–11; 4:9); "the joy of the LORD is your strength" (8:10); public reading and explanation of Scripture (8); confession (9); covenant renewal (10); recurring backsliding (13).
outline: 3–7 Building the wall amid opposition; lists
8–10 Ezra reads the law; confession; covenant
11–12 Repopulation of Jerusalem; dedication of the wall
intros.christ: Nehemiah, who left a royal palace to restore the broken city of God's people and bore opposition, offers a faint picture of Christ, who left heaven to rebuild His people. The decree to rebuild Jerusalem is often taken as the starting point of Daniel's "seventy weeks" leading to "Messiah the Prince" (Dan 9:25), though which decree is meant is debated.
debated: Chronological relation to Ezra (see Ezra).
Composition and extent of the "Nehemiah memoir."

intros.author: Anonymous. Jewish tradition suggested the men of the Great Synagogue or Mordecai (cf. 9:20). The author knows Persian court customs and vocabulary well.
intros.date: Events in the reign of Ahasuerus, generally identified with Xerxes I (486–465 BC), c. 483–473 BC. Composition: traditionally soon after (late 5th century BC); critical scholars range from the late Persian to the Hellenistic period (4th–2nd centuries BC).
intros.audience: Jews in the Persian diaspora and in Judah; the book explains the origin of the feast of Purim.
intros.setting: The Persian royal citadel of Susa (Shushan), between the first return (538 BC) and Ezra's return (458 BC). Most Jews had remained in the empire rather than return to Judah.
intros.empires: The Persian Empire at its height, stretching "from India unto Ethiopia" (1:1). Xerxes I is known for his failed invasion of Greece (480–479 BC), which may fall between chapters 1 and 2.
intros.genre: Historical narrative, carefully structured with reversals and banquets. The Hebrew text never mentions God by name; the Greek version (Septuagint) adds prayers and religious passages (the "Additions to Esther," among the Apocrypha).
intros.purpose: To show the preservation of God's people from destruction through an amazing chain of "coincidences," and to establish Purim.
intros.themes: Hidden providence ("who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" 4:14); reversal (Haman hanged on his own gallows); courage; the survival of the Jews; feasting and remembrance.
outline: 1–2 Vashti deposed; Esther made queen; Mordecai uncovers a plot
3–5 Haman's decree; Mordecai and Esther act
8–10 The counter-decree; the Jews' deliverance; Purim established
intros.christ: By preserving the Jewish people from annihilation, God preserved the line through whom the Messiah would come. Esther, who risked her life to intercede for her condemned people ("if I perish, I perish," 4:16), gives a faint picture of Christ who gave His life to save His people.
debated: Historicity — Traditional: real history. Critical: a historical novella; objections include that Xerxes' known queen was Amestris and that a Jewish queen is not mentioned in Greek sources; defenders respond that Persian kings had several wives, and point to accurate details of Persian court life (e.g., the royal courier system and the recording of the king's benefactors, both also described by the Greek historian Herodotus).

Canonicity — Esther was questioned by some in early Judaism and the early church (it is absent among the Dead Sea Scrolls); Luther himself expressed doubts about the book (e.g., in The Bondage of the Will, 1525, and in his Table Talk), though he retained it in his Bible.

intros.author: Unknown. Jewish tradition (Baba Bathra 14b–15a) offers Moses; other suggestions include Job himself, Elihu, Solomon, or an unknown sage. The book itself does not say.
intros.date: The setting appears patriarchal: Job offers sacrifices as head of his family, his wealth is counted in livestock, and he lives about 140 years after his trials (42:16). Dates proposed for the writing range from the time of Moses or Solomon (10th century BC) to the exile or later (6th–4th centuries BC). There is no consensus.
intros.audience: God's people of every age wrestling with suffering; the book's international, non-Israelite setting gives it a universal reach.
intros.setting: The land of Uz, probably in Edom or northern Arabia (cf. Lam 4:21), outside Israel. Job is not an Israelite, yet he fears God.
intros.empires: No empire. Raiding Sabeans and Chaldeans (1:15, 17) reflect a world of nomadic tribes rather than imperial armies.
intros.genre: Wisdom literature: a prose prologue (1–2) and epilogue (42:7–17) framing extended Hebrew poetry (dialogues, speeches, and God's speeches from the whirlwind). Its Hebrew is among the most difficult in the Old Testament.
intros.purpose: To confront the problem of the suffering of the righteous, to refute the simple doctrine that all suffering is a direct punishment for specific sin, and to lead the sufferer to trust and worship the sovereign Creator even without explanation.
intros.themes: Suffering and God's sovereignty; the limits of human wisdom (28); the failure of the friends' retribution theology; Job's honest lament; God's majesty in creation (38–41); the Redeemer ("I know that my redeemer liveth," 19:25); restoration.
outline: 1–2 Prologue: Job's piety, Satan's challenge, Job's losses
4–27 Three cycles of dialogue with Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar
38:1–42:6 The LORD speaks from the whirlwind; Job repents
42:7–17 Epilogue: the friends rebuked, Job restored
intros.christ: Job longs for a mediator ("daysman," 9:33) and an advocate in heaven (16:19–21), and confesses a living Redeemer who will stand upon the earth (19:25–27). Christ is that Mediator, the truly innocent sufferer whose suffering was for others. James 5:11 points to Job's patience and "the end of the Lord."
debated: Date and authorship — Traditional: the events are patriarchal-era, and some Jewish tradition named Moses as writer; others place writing in Solomon's time. Main critical view: an anonymous author writing between the 7th and 4th centuries BC, with debate over whether the Elihu speeches (32–37) and the wisdom poem (28) were added.
Historicity — a real man (Ezek 14:14 and James 5:11 name him alongside Noah and Daniel; traditional view) vs. a didactic story built around a traditional figure.
Unity — whether the Elihu speeches (32–37) and the hymn of chapter 28 are original or later additions.
Translation of 19:25–27 — whether Job expects vindication after death in bodily form ("in my flesh shall I see God," traditional and Lutheran reading) or "apart from my flesh."

intros.author: Many authors over many centuries. Superscriptions name David (73 psalms in the Hebrew text), Asaph (12), the sons of Korah (11), Solomon (2), Moses (Psalm 90), Heman, and Ethan; about 50 are anonymous. The New Testament cites David as the author of several psalms (e.g., Acts 2:25; 4:25; Rom 4:6).
intros.date: From the time of Moses (Ps 90, traditionally) through David's reign (c. 1000 BC) to the exile and after (e.g., Ps 137). The collection reached its final form after the exile, perhaps 4th–3rd centuries BC.
intros.audience: Israel at worship, in the temple and in private prayer; the Church's prayer book ever since.
intros.setting: Worship at the tabernacle and temple, the life of David, national crises, the exile, and the return.
intros.empires: Various psalms reflect wars with neighboring nations and, in the later psalms, the catastrophe of the Babylonian conquest (74, 79, 137).
intros.genre: Hebrew poetry, built on parallelism; types include hymns of praise, laments (individual and communal), thanksgiving songs, royal psalms, wisdom psalms, penitential psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143), and psalms of ascent (120–134). The KJV, following the Hebrew, includes the superscriptions in verse 1 or before it.
intros.purpose: To give God's people inspired words for praise, lament, confession, trust and thanksgiving in every circumstance of life.
intros.themes: The LORD's kingship; His steadfast love (hesed) and faithfulness; the blessedness of the righteous and the way of the wicked (1); the Messiah-King (2, 110); confession and forgiveness (32, 51, 130); trust in suffering (22, 23); the Word of God (19, 119); creation; Zion.
outline: Book V 107–150 (each book ends with a doxology; Psalm 150 concludes the whole)
intros.christ: Jesus said that the Psalms speak of Him (Luke 24:44). He prayed Psalm 22 on the cross ("My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?") and committed His spirit with Psalm 31:5. Psalm 2 (the Son), 16 (resurrection, Acts 2:25–31), 110 (David's Lord, priest after Melchizedek; Matt 22:44; Heb 7), and 118 (the rejected stone) are applied to Christ in the New Testament. Luther wrote that the Psalter "might well be called a little Bible" (see his Preface to the Psalter).
debated: Reliability of the superscriptions — Traditional: ancient and trustworthy (the New Testament cites Davidic authorship). Many critical scholars: later additions of uncertain value.

Messianic interpretation — direct prophecy of Christ (traditional, following the New Testament) vs. royal psalms referring first to Israel's kings and later reapplied; many interpreters hold both (typology).
Imprecatory psalms (e.g., 109, 137) and how Christians pray them.

intros.author: Mainly Solomon (1:1; 10:1; 25:1; cf. 1 Kings 4:32, which credits him with 3,000 proverbs). Other contributors are named: "the wise" (22:17; 24:23), Agur son of Jakeh (30), and King Lemuel (31:1–9). Hezekiah's scribes copied out a collection of Solomon's proverbs (25:1).
intros.date: Solomon's proverbs c. 970–930 BC; Hezekiah's edition c. 700 BC; final form possibly later. Some critical scholars date the collection, especially chapters 1–9, to the post-exilic period.
intros.audience: Primarily young men being trained ("my son"), and by extension all of God's people.
intros.setting: The royal court and households of Israel in the monarchy. Wisdom literature was an international genre; Proverbs 22:17–24:22 shows notable similarities to the Egyptian "Instruction of Amenemope."
intros.empires: Egypt's long wisdom tradition is the literary background; no empire acts in the book.
intros.genre: Wisdom literature: longer instructional poems (1–9), then collections of short two-line sayings, numerical sayings (30), and an acrostic poem on the virtuous woman (31:10–31).
intros.purpose: To impart wisdom for godly and skillful living, grounded in "the fear of the LORD," which "is the beginning of knowledge" (1:7).
intros.themes: The fear of the LORD; Wisdom personified (8); the two ways of wisdom and folly; speech; diligence and laziness; wealth and poverty; family; justice; the limits of human planning ("A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps," 16:9).
outline: 1–9 A father's instructions; Wisdom and Folly personified
25–29 Solomon's proverbs copied by Hezekiah's men
31 Words of Lemuel; the virtuous woman
intros.christ: Christ is "the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24, 30), "in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Col 2:3). Wisdom present with God at creation (8:22–31) was read by the church fathers as speaking of the eternal Son (though the passage was debated in the Arian controversy). The proverbs, as God's Law, describe the righteous life which only Christ perfectly lived and which He works in believers.
debated: Date of collection and of chapters 1–9.
Relation to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope — dependence of Proverbs on Amenemope (majority view), of Amenemope on Hebrew sources (minority), or common tradition.
Interpretation of Proverbs 8 — personification of a divine attribute vs. direct reference to the pre-incarnate Son.

intros.author: "The Preacher (Qoheleth), the son of David, king in Jerusalem" (1:1). Traditional Jewish and Christian view: Solomon, probably in his old age. Most modern scholars, including many conservatives, think the author was a later sage writing in Solomon's persona, citing late Hebrew vocabulary (including possible Persian loanwords) and the statement "I was king" (1:12).
intros.date: If Solomonic, c. 935 BC. Otherwise most scholars place it between the 5th and 3rd centuries BC.
intros.audience: Israelites seeking meaning in life, and especially those tempted to find it "under the sun" in wisdom, pleasure, work or wealth.
intros.setting: Life "under the sun," viewed from the perspective of royal wealth and wisdom.
intros.empires: No empire is named. If the book is late, it reflects the world of Persian or early Hellenistic rule.
intros.genre: Wisdom literature: reflective essays, proverbs, and poetry (e.g., the poem on old age, 12:1–7).
intros.purpose: To expose the emptiness ("vanity," Hebrew hebel, "vapor, breath") of life apart from God, and to commend receiving life as God's gift with joy, fearing God and keeping His commandments (12:13–14).
intros.themes: Vanity; the limits of wisdom; death as the great leveler; time and seasons ("To every thing there is a season," 3:1); enjoying God's gifts (2:24; 9:7–10); the fear of God; coming judgment.
outline: 1:12–6:12 The search for meaning: wisdom, pleasure, work, wealth
7:1–12:8 Counsel for living under the sun; the poem on old age
12:9–14 Epilogue: fear God and keep His commandments
intros.christ: Ecclesiastes shows the futility of a world subjected to vanity after the fall (cf. Rom 8:20, where Paul uses the same Greek word as the Septuagint of Ecclesiastes). Christ, "one shepherd" (12:11), brings meaning and victory where the Preacher finds only death; in Him our "labour is not in vain in the Lord" (1 Cor 15:58).
debated: Authorship and date — Solomon (traditional) vs. a later writer in Solomon's persona (most modern scholars, including many conservatives; Luther himself, in his Table Talk, suggested the book was compiled later).
Tone — pessimistic skepticism corrected by an orthodox epilogue (some critical scholars) vs. a unified work leading the reader from the emptiness of life without God to faith and joy (traditional).

intros.author: The title, "The song of songs, which is Solomon's" (1:1), may mean "by," "for," or "about" Solomon. Traditionally Solomon (cf. 1 Kings 4:32, 1,005 songs). Many modern scholars see an anonymous collection of love poetry.
intros.date: If Solomonic, 10th century BC. Others date it from the late monarchy to the post-exilic period on linguistic grounds.
intros.audience: Israel; read at Passover in later Jewish practice.
intros.setting: The countryside and royal court of Israel: vineyards, gardens, Jerusalem, Lebanon, Tirzah (6:4, a northern capital before Samaria, which some take as evidence of an early date).
intros.empires: None.
intros.genre: Lyric love poetry, in dialogue between a bride (the Shulamite), a bridegroom, and the "daughters of Jerusalem."
intros.purpose: To celebrate the love between a man and a woman within God's good gift of marriage; and, as Jewish and Christian interpreters have long read it, to picture the love between God and His people (Christ and His Church).
intros.themes: Love "strong as death" (8:6); longing, union, and faithfulness; the goodness of created beauty and marital love; waiting ("stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please," 2:7).
intros.christ: The church fathers and medieval interpreters, and many Lutherans after them, read the Song as an allegory of Christ and His Church (cf. Eph 5:25–32; Rev 19:7). Luther himself, in his lectures, read it in terms of God's care for His people under Solomon's government. Even read literally, the faithful love of bridegroom and bride points to the Bridegroom who gave Himself for His bride.
debated: Interpretation — allegorical/typological (God and Israel; Christ and the Church; the dominant view through most of history) vs. literal love poetry (most modern scholars), with many holding a literal sense that also points to Christ.
Number of characters — two (Solomon and the Shulamite) vs. three (a shepherd lover resisting Solomon).
Authorship and date — Traditional: Solomon (1:1). Main critical view: an anthology of love poems collected later, with "of Solomon" read as "dedicated to/about Solomon."

intros.author: Isaiah son of Amoz (1:1), who prophesied in Jerusalem from c. 740 BC (the year of Uzziah's death, 6:1) to at least 701 BC and perhaps into Manasseh's reign. The New Testament quotes passages from all parts of the book as Isaiah's (e.g., John 12:38–41 quotes 53:1 and 6:10).
intros.date: Traditional: c. 740–680 BC. Critical: chapters 1–39 largely from Isaiah of Jerusalem (8th century), 40–55 from an anonymous prophet in the Babylonian exile ("Second Isaiah," c. 540 BC), and 56–66 from the post-exilic period ("Third Isaiah").
intros.audience: Judah and Jerusalem in the 8th century BC; and, in chapters 40–66, the exiles and the restored community (whether as future readers foreseen by Isaiah or as contemporary hearers in the critical view).
intros.setting: Judah under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah: the Syro-Ephraimite war (734 BC, Isa 7), the fall of Samaria (722 BC), and Sennacherib's invasion and the deliverance of Jerusalem (701 BC, Isa 36–37). Chapters 40–66 look ahead to the exile and to Cyrus (44:28; 45:1).
intros.empires: Neo-Assyria (Tiglath-pileser III, Sargon II, Sennacherib) is "the rod of mine anger" (10:5). Egypt is the false hope of Judah (30–31). Babylon is foreseen as the next empire and its fall announced (13–14; 47). Persia's Cyrus is named as God's "anointed" instrument to free the exiles (45:1).
intros.genre: Prophetic oracles in poetry and prose, historical narrative (36–39, parallel to 2 Kings 18–20), oracles against nations (13–23), apocalyptic-style visions (24–27), and the Servant Songs (42:1–9; 49:1–13; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12).
intros.purpose: To call Judah to repentance and faith in the Holy One of Israel, to announce judgment, and to proclaim comfort, salvation, and the coming of the Messiah and of new heavens and a new earth.
intros.themes: The holiness of God ("Holy, holy, holy," 6:3); faith versus reliance on human powers ("If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established," 7:9); judgment and remnant; Immanuel; the Messianic King (9, 11); comfort (40); the Suffering Servant; salvation for the nations; new creation (65–66).
outline: 1–12 Judgment and hope for Judah; Isaiah's call; Immanuel
40–48 Comfort: God's sovereignty over the nations; Cyrus
58–66 True worship, glory of Zion, new heavens and new earth
intros.christ: Isaiah has been called "the fifth Gospel." The virgin's son Immanuel (7:14; Matt 1:23), the child called "The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace" (9:6), the shoot from Jesse (11:1), the voice in the wilderness (40:3; fulfilled in John the Baptist), and the Servant "wounded for our transgressions" (53:5; Acts 8:32–35) all point to Christ. Jesus began His ministry reading Isaiah 61:1–2 (Luke 4:18–21).
debated: Unity and authorship — Traditional: one prophet, Isaiah, who by divine revelation foresaw the exile and named Cyrus about 150 years in advance. Critical: two or three authors/collections ("Proto-," "Deutero-," "Trito-Isaiah"). Arguments include shifts in setting, style and theme; defenders of unity point to shared vocabulary ("the Holy One of Israel" throughout), the Dead Sea Isaiah scroll presenting it as one book, and New Testament attribution.

7:14 — Hebrew 'almah means "young woman of marriageable age"; the Septuagint and Matthew render "virgin." Whether the sign had an immediate fulfillment in Ahaz's day as well as its fulfillment in Christ is debated among conservatives.
Identity of the Servant — Israel, the prophet, or an individual; the New Testament identifies the Servant of chapter 53 with Jesus.

intros.author: Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, a priest from Anathoth (1:1), who dictated much of his message to his scribe Baruch (36:4, 32). A clay bulla (seal impression) reading "Berechyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe" has been published and is often linked to Baruch, though some question its authenticity.
intros.date: Jeremiah's ministry ran from the 13th year of Josiah (627 BC) to after the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC), ending in Egypt. Collection and editing continued during the exile.
intros.audience: Judah and Jerusalem in their final decades; the exiles in Babylon (29); the remnant who fled to Egypt (43–44).
intros.setting: Josiah's reform (622 BC), the rise of Babylon, Josiah's death (609 BC), the reigns of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, the sieges and fall of Jerusalem, and the aftermath.
intros.empires: Assyria's collapse (Nineveh fell in 612 BC); Egypt's brief control of Judah under Necho II; the Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar II, which defeated Egypt at Carchemish (605 BC) and destroyed Jerusalem (586 BC). Jeremiah counseled submission to Babylon as God's judgment.
intros.genre: Prophetic oracles (poetry and prose), biographical narrative, personal laments ("confessions"), symbolic acts, a letter (29), oracles against nations (46–51), and a historical appendix (52). The Greek (Septuagint) text is about one-eighth shorter and arranged differently; Dead Sea fragments attest both forms.
intros.purpose: To warn Judah of judgment for covenant-breaking and idolatry, to call for repentance, and to promise restoration and a new covenant after seventy years of exile.
intros.themes: Covenant unfaithfulness; false prophets ("Peace, peace; when there is no peace," 6:14); the deceitful heart (17:9); the potter and the clay (18); seventy years of exile (25:11; 29:10); the righteous Branch; the new covenant (31:31–34); the cost of faithful ministry.
outline: 26–29 Conflict with false prophets; letter to the exiles
30–33 The book of consolation: new covenant
34–45 Events before and after Jerusalem's fall
52 Historical appendix: the fall of Jerusalem
intros.christ: The promised "righteous Branch" of David is named "THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS" (23:5–6). The new covenant, in which God forgives sins and writes His law on hearts (31:31–34), is instituted by Christ in His blood (Luke 22:20; Heb 8). Jeremiah, the rejected and suffering prophet who wept over Jerusalem, foreshadows Jesus (Matt 16:14).
debated: The relationship of the shorter Septuagint text to the longer Hebrew (Masoretic) text — two editions, with scholars debating priority.
The extent of later editorial ("Deuteronomistic") prose in the book (critical view) vs. substantially Jeremiah's own words recorded by Baruch (traditional).
The seventy years — counted from 605 BC to 539/538 BC, from 586 to 516/515 BC (temple rebuilt), or as a round number.

intros.author: Anonymous in the Hebrew text. The Septuagint introduction and long Jewish and Christian tradition ascribe it to Jeremiah (cf. 2 Chr 35:25, which mentions laments by Jeremiah). Many modern scholars think it was written by one or more other eyewitnesses.
intros.date: Shortly after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, before the return (538 BC); vivid detail suggests eyewitness composition.
intros.audience: The survivors in Judah and the exiles grieving the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple.
intros.setting: The ruins of Jerusalem after the Babylonian siege: famine, death, the burned temple, the captivity of king and people.
intros.empires: The Neo-Babylonian Empire, whose armies destroyed the city (586 BC). Edom rejoiced in Judah's fall (4:21–22).
intros.genre: Poetic laments (dirges). Chapters 1–4 are acrostics following the Hebrew alphabet (chapter 3 with three verses per letter); chapter 5 has 22 verses but is not acrostic. Many lines use the limping "qinah" meter of mourning.
intros.purpose: To give voice to grief, to confess that the disaster was God's just judgment for sin, and to cling to God's mercy in the midst of devastation.
intros.themes: Grief and lament; sin and judgment; God's faithfulness ("It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed... great is thy faithfulness," 3:22–23); waiting quietly for salvation; prayer for restoration.
intros.christ: "Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow" (1:12) has long been applied in Christian worship (especially Holy Week) to Christ's Passion. Christ bore the wrath that Lamentations describes, and in Him God's compassions "fail not."
debated: Authorship — Jeremiah (traditional) vs. other eyewitness poets (many modern scholars), noting differences in style and perspective from Jeremiah's book.
Whether the five poems come from one or several authors.

intros.author: Ezekiel son of Buzi, a priest (1:3), deported to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC. Written largely in the first person, with precise dates.
intros.date: Prophetic ministry from 593 BC (1:2, the fifth year of Jehoiachin's captivity) to at least 571 BC (29:17). Composition during the exile.
intros.audience: The Judean exiles in Babylonia, who at first expected a quick return and refused to believe Jerusalem would fall; after 586 BC, a despairing people needing hope.
intros.setting: The exiles' settlement at Tel-abib by the river Chebar (a canal near Nippur) in Babylonia. Ezekiel's visions transport him to Jerusalem (8–11).
intros.empires: The Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nebuchadnezzar II; Egypt (Pharaoh Hophra) as a broken reed (29); Tyre, besieged by Nebuchadnezzar for 13 years (26–28; 29:18); and the surrounding nations.
intros.genre: Prophecy in prose and poetry, visions, symbolic actions (e.g., lying on his side, 4), allegories (16, 23), lament, and the detailed temple vision (40–48) with apocalyptic features (38–39).
intros.purpose: To show that Jerusalem's fall was God's just judgment, that God's glory had departed from the defiled temple, and that God would restore His people with a new heart, a new spirit, a Davidic shepherd, and His renewed presence.
intros.themes: The glory of the LORD (1; 10–11; 43); individual responsibility (18); God's holiness and the defilement of His sanctuary; "they shall know that I am the LORD" (over 60 times); the watchman (3; 33); the good shepherd (34); new heart and spirit (36:26); the valley of dry bones (37); the river of life from the temple (47).
outline: 1–3 Ezekiel's call and vision of God's glory
4–24 Judgment on Jerusalem and Judah; the glory departs
33–39 Restoration: watchman, shepherd, dry bones, Gog and Magog
40–48 Vision of the new temple and land
intros.christ: Christ is the Good Shepherd, the true David promised in 34:23–24 (John 10). The giving of a new heart and spirit (36:25–27) is fulfilled through Baptism and the Holy Spirit (John 3:5; Titus 3:5). The river flowing from the temple (47) is echoed in Jesus' promise of living water (John 7:37–39) and in Revelation 22:1–2; God's dwelling among His people ("The LORD is there," 48:35) is fulfilled in Christ.
debated: Unity — the book is widely accepted as substantially Ezekiel's, though some critics propose extensive later editing.

The temple vision (40–48) — a literal future temple (dispensational interpretation), an idealized program for the post-exilic restoration, or a symbolic picture of God's presence with His people fulfilled in Christ and the Church (common Lutheran and Reformed reading).
Gog and Magog (38–39) — identification of the figures and time.

intros.author: Daniel, a Judean exile in Babylon (deported 605 BC), who speaks in the first person in chapters 7–12. Jesus refers to "Daniel the prophet" (Matt 24:15). The book is written partly in Hebrew (1:1–2:4a; 8–12) and partly in Aramaic (2:4b–7:28).
intros.date: Traditional: 6th century BC, completed shortly after 536 BC (10:1). Critical: completed c. 167–164 BC during the persecution of the Jews by the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes, with the court stories (1–6) older.
intros.audience: Jewish exiles under foreign rule (traditional), or Jews persecuted under Antiochus IV (critical): in both cases, faithful people living under hostile empires.
intros.setting: The Babylonian court of Nebuchadnezzar (605–562 BC) and Belshazzar, and the early Persian period under "Darius the Mede" and Cyrus (539–536 BC).
intros.empires: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece (Alexander and his successors, especially the Seleucid kings of Syria and the Ptolemies of Egypt, the "kings of the north and south" of chapter 11), and a fourth kingdom — traditionally identified as Rome, in the critical view as the Greek kingdom. The visions of the statue (2) and of the four beasts (7) present successive world empires replaced by God's everlasting kingdom.
intros.genre: Court narratives (1–6) and apocalyptic visions (7–12), with symbolic beasts, angelic interpreters, and numbered periods.
intros.purpose: To assure God's people that the Most High rules over the kingdoms of men (4:17) and will give the everlasting kingdom to the Son of Man and His saints, and to encourage faithfulness under pressure.
intros.themes: God's sovereignty over empires; faithfulness under persecution (the fiery furnace, 3; the lions' den, 6); prayer (6; 9); the Son of Man (7:13–14); the seventy weeks (9:24–27); resurrection (12:2).
outline: 1 Daniel and friends faithful in Babylon
7 Four beasts and the Son of Man
9 Daniel's prayer and the seventy weeks
10–12 The final vision: kings of north and south; resurrection
intros.christ: Jesus' favorite title for Himself, "the Son of man," comes from Daniel 7:13–14, and He applied the vision of the Son of Man coming with the clouds to Himself before the high priest (Mark 14:62). The stone "cut out without hands" that becomes a mountain (2:34–35, 44) has been read as Christ's kingdom. The seventy weeks (9:24–27), which speak of "Messiah the Prince" being "cut off," have traditionally been understood as pointing to Christ's death.
debated: Date and authorship — Traditional: 6th-century Daniel, with predictive prophecy reaching to the Greek period and to Christ. Critical: a 2nd-century BC work whose detailed "predictions" of the Seleucid-Ptolemaic wars (11) were written as history up to c. 165 BC. Arguments include the Greek loanwords (musical instruments), the late Aramaic, the precision of chapter 11; defenders cite Daniel's presence among the Dead Sea Scrolls soon after the proposed date, Ezekiel's mention of a Daniel (14:14), and Jesus' words.

Historical questions — the identity of "Darius the Mede" (not known from other sources; proposals include Gubaru or Cyrus himself) and Belshazzar's title "king" (Babylonian texts confirm he ruled as co-regent with his father Nabonidus, which once seemed a decisive objection).
The four kingdoms (Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece, Rome — traditional; or Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece — critical).
Interpretation of the seventy weeks (9:24–27).

intros.author: Hosea son of Beeri (1:1), the only writing prophet from the Northern Kingdom of Israel.
intros.date: Ministry c. 755–715 BC, during the reigns of Jeroboam II of Israel and Uzziah through Hezekiah of Judah (1:1). The book was preserved and probably edited in Judah after the fall of Samaria (722 BC).
intros.audience: The Northern Kingdom of Israel (often called "Ephraim"), with occasional words to Judah.
intros.setting: Prosperity under Jeroboam II gave way to rapid decline: after his death six kings reigned in about 25 years, four of them assassinated, ending with the Assyrian conquest of Samaria. Baal worship and calf worship at Bethel and Dan were widespread.
intros.empires: The Neo-Assyrian Empire, expanding under Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 BC); Israel's kings vacillated between submitting to Assyria and seeking help from Egypt ("like a silly dove," 7:11).
intros.genre: Prophetic poetry and prose; narrative of Hosea's marriage (1–3) followed by oracles. The Hebrew text is notoriously difficult.
intros.purpose: To expose Israel's spiritual adultery against the LORD, to announce judgment, and to proclaim God's unquenchable, redeeming love that will restore His unfaithful people.
intros.themes: The marriage covenant as a picture of God and Israel; harlotry and idolatry; lack of the knowledge of God (4:6); God's covenant love ("I desired mercy, and not sacrifice," 6:6); return and healing (14).
outline: 1–3 Hosea's marriage to Gomer as a living parable
14 Call to repentance and promise of healing
intros.christ: Hosea buying back his unfaithful wife (3) pictures Christ redeeming His Church at the cost of His own life. "Out of Egypt have I called my son" (11:1) is fulfilled in Jesus (Matt 2:15). Paul quotes 1:10 and 2:23 of the calling of the Gentiles (Rom 9:25–26), and the taunt "O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction" (13:14) of the resurrection victory (1 Cor 15:55).
debated: Gomer — whether she was already a harlot when Hosea married her or became unfaithful later; and whether the marriage was literal (majority view) or a visionary allegory.
Extent of later Judean editing (critical view).

intros.author: Joel son of Pethuel (1:1); nothing else is known about him.
intros.date: Uncertain; there are no kings named. Proposals range from the 9th century BC (during the minority of King Joash, c. 835 BC, explaining the absence of a king and the prominence of priests and elders) to the post-exilic period (c. 400 BC). The canonical placement among 8th-century prophets suggests an early date to the compilers.
intros.audience: The people of Judah and Jerusalem, especially priests and elders.
intros.setting: A devastating locust plague and drought, which Joel interprets as a warning of the coming "day of the LORD."
intros.empires: No world empire is named; Tyre, Sidon, Philistia (3:4), Egypt and Edom (3:19) are mentioned, and the selling of Judeans to the "Grecians" (Ionians, 3:6).
intros.genre: Prophetic poetry: lament, call to repentance, and promise.
intros.purpose: To call Judah to repentance in view of the day of the LORD, and to promise restoration and the outpouring of the Spirit.
intros.themes: The day of the LORD; true repentance ("rend your heart, and not your garments," 2:13); God's grace and compassion; restoration of "the years that the locust hath eaten" (2:25); the Spirit poured out on all flesh (2:28–32); judgment of the nations in the valley of Jehoshaphat.
outline: 1 The locust plague and call to lament
2:1–17 The coming army and call to repentance
2:18–32 The LORD's response: restoration and the Spirit
3 Judgment of the nations and blessing of Judah
intros.christ: On Pentecost, Peter declared Joel 2:28–32 fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit by the risen Christ (Acts 2:16–21). Paul cites "whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered" (2:32) of faith in Christ (Rom 10:13).
debated: Date — 9th century vs. post-exilic (with intermediate proposals).
Whether the locusts of chapter 2 are literal locusts or a figurative human army.

intros.author: Amos, a herdsman and "gatherer of sycomore fruit" from Tekoa in Judah (1:1; 7:14), sent to prophesy in the Northern Kingdom.
intros.date: c. 760–750 BC, "two years before the earthquake" (1:1) in the reign of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel. Archaeological evidence for a major earthquake around 760 BC has been found at Hazor and other sites.
intros.audience: The Northern Kingdom of Israel, especially the wealthy of Samaria and the worshipers at the royal sanctuary of Bethel.
intros.setting: A time of national prosperity, territorial expansion, and religious activity, combined with oppression of the poor, corrupt courts, and luxury ("ivory houses," 3:15; ivory inlays have been excavated at Samaria).
intros.empires: Assyria was temporarily weak (allowing Israel's expansion under Jeroboam II), but Amos foresaw exile "beyond Damascus" (5:27), fulfilled by Assyria in 722 BC. The book opens with oracles against Damascus (Aram), Gaza (Philistia), Tyre, Edom, Ammon and Moab.
intros.genre: Prophetic oracles, visions (7–9), a short narrative of conflict with the priest Amaziah (7:10–17), and hymn fragments.
intros.purpose: To announce God's judgment on Israel for social injustice and empty worship, and to call for true repentance, while concluding with a promise of restoration.
intros.themes: Social justice ("let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream," 5:24); privilege brings responsibility (3:2); the day of the LORD as darkness, not light (5:18); empty ritual; a famine of hearing the word of the LORD (8:11); the raising of David's fallen tabernacle (9:11).
outline: 1–2 Oracles against the nations, climaxing with Israel
intros.christ: At the Jerusalem council James cited Amos 9:11–12 — the raising up of David's fallen tabernacle so that the Gentiles seek the Lord — as fulfilled in the inclusion of the Gentiles in Christ's Church (Acts 15:15–17).
debated: Authenticity of the closing promise (9:11–15) and the oracles against Tyre, Edom and Judah — regarded by some critics as later additions; defended by others as integral, since prophets regularly join judgment and hope.

intros.author: Obadiah ("servant of the LORD"); otherwise unknown. Several Old Testament figures share the name.
intros.date: Most likely shortly after the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, when Edom gloated over and plundered Judah (cf. Ps 137:7; Lam 4:21–22). Some propose an earlier date (c. 845 BC, during an Edomite revolt under Jehoram, 2 Kings 8:20–22). Verses 1–9 closely parallel Jeremiah 49:7–22.
intros.audience: Judah, comforted by the announcement of judgment on Edom; the oracle is addressed to Edom.
intros.setting: The rocky, mountainous land of Edom south and east of the Dead Sea, with strongholds like Sela (later Petra), which made Edom feel secure ("thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock," v. 3).
intros.empires: Babylon, whose conquest of Jerusalem Edom exploited. Edom itself was later overrun by Arab tribes and the Nabateans, and by the intertestamental period the Edomites (Idumeans) lived in southern Judea and were forcibly converted by the Hasmonean John Hyrcanus; Herod the Great was an Idumean.
intros.genre: Prophetic oracle against a nation (the shortest book of the Old Testament, 21 verses).
intros.purpose: To announce God's judgment on Edom for pride and violence against its brother Jacob, and to promise the restoration of God's people and kingdom.
intros.themes: Pride before a fall (v. 3–4); brotherhood betrayed (Esau and Jacob, Gen 25–27); "as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee" (v. 15); the day of the LORD on all nations; "the kingdom shall be the LORD'S" (v. 21).
outline: 15–21 The day of the LORD: judgment on nations, restoration of Israel
intros.christ: The "saviours" who will come up on Mount Zion and the kingdom that "shall be the LORD'S" (v. 21) point to Christ, the Savior through whom God's kingdom comes and in whom even the nations are gathered.
debated: Date — after 586 BC (majority) vs. 9th century BC.
Relationship to Jeremiah 49 — which borrowed from which, or whether both use a common older oracle.

intros.author: Anonymous; the book is about Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet from Gath-hepher in Zebulun, who prophesied the expansion of Israel under Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25). Traditionally Jonah himself is regarded as the source.
intros.date: Jonah's ministry c. 785–760 BC. Composition: traditionally 8th century BC; many critical scholars date it to the post-exilic period (5th–4th centuries BC).
