intros.audience: Israel, confronted with God's mercy toward the nations, even Israel's enemies.
intros.setting: Joppa, the Mediterranean Sea, and Nineveh, the great Assyrian city on the Tigris (later Assyria's capital under Sennacherib).
intros.empires: The Neo-Assyrian Empire, a feared and brutal power. In the early 8th century BC Assyria suffered internal weakness, plague, and revolt, and a solar eclipse in 763 BC was regarded as an evil omen — conditions some scholars think could have made Nineveh receptive to a prophet's warning.
intros.genre: Narrative about a prophet, with a psalm of thanksgiving (2).
intros.purpose: To reveal God's sovereign compassion for all nations, to rebuke the narrow and resentful heart that begrudges mercy to enemies, and to show that "Salvation is of the LORD" (2:9).
intros.themes: God's sovereignty over nature (storm, fish, plant, worm); repentance (of sailors and Ninevites); God "gracious... and merciful, slow to anger" (4:2); the prophet's disobedience and anger; God's concern for the "sixscore thousand persons" and "much cattle" of Nineveh (4:11).
intros.christ: Jesus pointed to "the sign of the prophet Jonas": "as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matt 12:39–41). Jesus is "greater than Jonas," who willingly gave Himself into death to save Gentiles and Jews alike.
debated: Genre — historical narrative (traditional; Jesus treats Nineveh's repentance as a real event, Matt 12:41) vs. parable or didactic story (many modern scholars).
Nineveh's repentance is not recorded in Assyrian sources; defenders note that such records are incomplete and point to the conditions of the period.

Date of composition — Traditional: by Jonah or a near contemporary in the 8th century BC (2 Kings 14:25). Main critical view: post-exilic (5th–4th century BC), often read as a didactic story rather than history; Jesus treats Jonah's sign as real (Matt 12:39–41).

intros.author: Micah of Moresheth (1:1), a town in the Judean lowlands (Shephelah) near Gath; a contemporary of Isaiah.
intros.date: Ministry c. 735–700 BC, in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:1). Jeremiah 26:18–19 records that Micah's prophecy of Jerusalem's ruin (3:12) led Hezekiah to repent.
intros.audience: Both Samaria and Jerusalem, especially their leaders, judges, priests and false prophets.
intros.setting: The Assyrian advance: the fall of Samaria (722 BC) and Sennacherib's devastating invasion of Judah's lowland towns (701 BC), including Lachish and probably Micah's own region (1:10–16).
intros.empires: Neo-Assyria (Tiglath-pileser III, Shalmaneser V, Sargon II, Sennacherib). Babylon is mentioned as the place of future exile and rescue (4:10), surprising in an Assyrian-era prophet.
intros.genre: Prophetic oracles in poetry, alternating judgment and hope, with a covenant lawsuit (6) and a closing psalm.
intros.purpose: To denounce injustice and false religion, to announce judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem, and to promise a remnant, a restored Zion, and a ruler from Bethlehem.
intros.themes: Oppression by the powerful; false prophets for hire; "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" (6:8); swords into plowshares (4:3); the ruler from Bethlehem; God who pardons iniquity and casts sins into the depths of the sea (7:18–19).
outline: 1–2 Judgment on Samaria and Judah; hope for a remnant
3–5 Corrupt leaders condemned; Zion's future; the ruler from Bethlehem
6–7 The LORD's lawsuit; lament; confidence in God's forgiveness
intros.christ: Micah 5:2 foretold that the ruler of Israel, "whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting," would come from Bethlehem Ephratah; the chief priests cited it when Herod asked where Christ should be born (Matt 2:5–6). The shepherd-king who will "stand and feed in the strength of the LORD" and "be the peace" (5:4–5) is Christ.
debated: Authorship of chapters 4–7, especially the hopeful passages — attributed by some critics to later (exilic or post-exilic) writers; defended as Micah's own by others.
The mention of Babylon (4:10) — predictive prophecy (traditional) vs. a later addition (critical).
Relationship of Micah 4:1–3 to the nearly identical Isaiah 2:2–4.

intros.author: Nahum the Elkoshite (1:1); the location of Elkosh is unknown (proposals in Galilee, Judah, and near Nineveh). The name Capernaum means "village of Nahum."
intros.date: Between the fall of Thebes (No-amon, 3:8) to Assyria in 663 BC and the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC; probably c. 650–620 BC.
intros.audience: Judah, under Assyrian domination, comforted by the announcement of Nineveh's fall.
intros.setting: Assyria at or just past the height of its power under Ashurbanipal; Judah under Manasseh or early Josiah as a vassal.
intros.empires: Neo-Assyria (capital Nineveh), notorious for cruelty to conquered peoples. Nineveh fell in 612 BC to a coalition of Babylonians and Medes; the city was so thoroughly destroyed that its site was later forgotten until excavated in the 19th century.
intros.genre: Prophetic oracle against a nation, in vivid poetry; the opening (1:2–8) is a partial acrostic hymn.
intros.purpose: To proclaim God's justice against Assyria and comfort for His oppressed people: the LORD is "slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked" (1:3).
intros.themes: God's jealousy and vengeance against the wicked; His goodness as "a strong hold in the day of trouble" (1:7); the downfall of proud oppressors; good tidings of peace (1:15).
outline: 1 The LORD's majesty and the judgment of Nineveh
2 The siege and fall of Nineveh
intros.christ: "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace!" (1:15; cf. Isa 52:7) is applied by Paul to the preachers of the Gospel of Christ (Rom 10:15). God's judgment of the world's oppressors is completed in Christ's victory over all enemies.
debated: Date within the range above.
The partial acrostic in chapter 1 — original artistry, or a later editorial addition.
The ethics of a book that rejoices at an enemy's destruction (understood in Scripture as rejoicing in God's justice).

intros.author: Habakkuk the prophet (1:1); nothing else is known of him. The apocryphal Bel and the Dragon tells a legend involving him.
intros.date: Probably c. 609–598 BC, as the Chaldeans (Babylonians) rose to power (1:6), around the battle of Carchemish (605 BC) and before the first deportations (597 BC).
intros.audience: Judah under King Jehoiakim, marked by violence and injustice.
intros.setting: Judah's moral decay after Josiah's reforms, and the approaching Babylonian invasion.
intros.empires: The Neo-Babylonian ("Chaldean") Empire under Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II, described as "that bitter and hasty nation" (1:6), God's instrument of judgment, itself to be judged.
intros.genre: A dialogue between the prophet and God (1–2), woes (2:6–20), and a psalm-prayer (3) with musical notations.
intros.purpose: To wrestle with the question of why God tolerates evil and how He can use a wicked nation to punish His own people, and to teach that "the just shall live by his faith" (2:4).
intros.themes: Theodicy (the justice of God); faith and patience ("though it tarry, wait for it," 2:3); the righteous living by faith; woe to oppressors; the earth filled with the knowledge of God's glory (2:14); joy in God when all else fails (3:17–19).
outline: 1:1–11 First complaint and God's answer (the Chaldeans are coming)
1:12–2:20 Second complaint and God's answer (the just shall live by faith; five woes)
3 Habakkuk's prayer and confession of trust
intros.christ: Habakkuk 2:4, "the just shall live by his faith," is quoted in Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11 and Hebrews 10:38, and became for Luther the key to the Gospel of justification by faith in Christ. "Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed" (3:13).
debated: The meaning of "faith" in 2:4 (Hebrew emunah, "faithfulness/steadfast trust") and its relation to Paul's use.
Whether chapter 3 was originally part of the book (the Dead Sea Habakkuk commentary covers only chapters 1–2, though this may reflect the commentator's interests).

intros.author: Zephaniah son of Cushi, whose genealogy goes back four generations to "Hizkiah" (1:1), probably King Hezekiah, making him of royal descent.
intros.date: In the reign of Josiah (640–609 BC), probably before or early in his reform of 622 BC, since idolatry is still openly practiced (1:4–6).
intros.audience: Judah and Jerusalem.
intros.setting: The aftermath of Manasseh's long, idolatrous reign; Baal worship, star worship on rooftops, and syncretism (swearing by the LORD and Malcham, 1:5).
intros.empires: Assyria in decline; Nineveh's coming desolation is announced (2:13–15). Philistia, Moab, Ammon, and Cush (Ethiopia) also receive oracles.
intros.genre: Prophetic oracles in poetry.
intros.purpose: To warn of the great and terrible day of the LORD against Judah and the nations, to call the humble to seek the LORD, and to promise a purified remnant in whom God rejoices.
intros.themes: The day of the LORD ("That day is a day of wrath," 1:15, the source of the medieval hymn "Dies irae"); seeking the LORD in meekness (2:3); judgment on the nations; a pure language for the peoples (3:9); God rejoicing over His people with singing (3:17).
outline: 1:1–2:3 The day of the LORD against Judah
3:9–20 The remnant restored; God's joy in His people
intros.christ: "The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save" (3:17) is fulfilled in Immanuel, God in the midst of His people. The gathering of the nations to call on the name of the LORD (3:9–10) anticipates the Gospel going to all peoples.
debated: Authenticity of the hopeful conclusion (3:14–20) and of some oracles against nations — later additions according to some critics, original according to others.
Whether "Hizkiah" in 1:1 is King Hezekiah.

intros.author: Haggai the prophet (1:1; Ezra 5:1; 6:14).
intros.date: Four dated messages within four months in the second year of Darius I: from the first day of the sixth month to the 24th day of the ninth month, 520 BC (late August to mid December 520 BC).
intros.audience: Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest, and the people of Jerusalem who had returned from exile.
intros.setting: About 18 years after the first return (538 BC), the foundation of the temple had been laid but work had stopped amid opposition and discouragement; people were building their own "cieled houses" while the temple lay waste.
intros.empires: The Persian Empire under Darius I (522–486 BC), who had just put down widespread revolts across the empire upon his accession. Haggai speaks of God shaking the heavens and the earth and overthrowing the thrones of kingdoms (2:6–7, 21–22).
intros.genre: Prophetic sermons in prose, precisely dated.
intros.purpose: To rouse the people to rebuild the temple, to encourage them with God's presence and promise of future glory, and to affirm God's choice of Zerubbabel.
intros.themes: Right priorities ("Consider your ways," 1:5, 7); God's presence ("I am with you," 1:13; 2:4); future glory of the temple ("the desire of all nations shall come," 2:7); holiness and defilement (2:10–19); Zerubbabel as God's signet ring (2:23).
outline: 1:1–15 Call to rebuild; the people obey
2:1–9 The glory of the latter house
intros.christ: The promise that the glory of this house would be greater than the former and that God would fill it with glory (2:7–9) has traditionally been understood to point to Christ's presence in the temple; Hebrews 12:26–28 applies the shaking of heaven and earth (2:6) to the unshakable kingdom we receive. Zerubbabel, of David's line, appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:12).
debated: Translation of 2:7 — "the desire of all nations shall come" (KJV, traditional messianic reading) vs. "the treasures of all nations shall come" (many modern versions, since the Hebrew verb is plural).
Whether Haggai expected Zerubbabel himself to become the messianic king.

intros.author: Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo (1:1), a prophet (and probably priest, cf. Neh 12:16) and contemporary of Haggai.
intros.date: Chapters 1–8 are dated 520–518 BC (second to fourth years of Darius I). Chapters 9–14 are undated and may come from later in Zechariah's life (traditional), or, according to many critical scholars, from other authors and periods (with proposals from the 8th century BC to the Greek period).
intros.audience: The returned exiles in Jerusalem rebuilding the temple.
intros.setting: The same as Haggai: the struggling post-exilic community under Persian rule; the temple was completed in 516/515 BC.
intros.empires: The Persian Empire (Darius I). Chapter 9 announces judgment on Syrian, Phoenician and Philistine cities and speaks of "thy sons, O Greece" (9:13), which some connect with Alexander the Great's campaigns (332 BC).
intros.genre: Night visions (1–6) with angelic interpreters, sermons (7–8), and two "burdens" or oracles (9–11; 12–14) with apocalyptic imagery.
intros.purpose: To encourage the people to complete the temple and to return to the LORD, and to reveal God's future plan: the coming King, the smitten Shepherd, cleansing from sin, and the LORD's universal reign.
intros.themes: "Turn ye unto me... and I will turn unto you" (1:3); God's jealous love for Zion; "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit" (4:6); the Branch who is priest and king (6:12–13); the humble King (9:9); the pierced one (12:10); a fountain for sin (13:1); the LORD king over all the earth (14:9).
outline: 1:7–6:15 Eight night visions; crowning of Joshua
7–8 Questions about fasting; promises to Zion
9–11 First burden: the coming King; the rejected Shepherd
12–14 Second burden: Jerusalem's deliverance; the pierced one; the day of the LORD
intros.christ: Zechariah is among the most quoted prophets in the Passion narratives: the King "lowly, and riding upon an ass" (9:9; Matt 21:5), the thirty pieces of silver (11:12–13; Matt 27:9–10), "they shall look upon me whom they have pierced" (12:10; John 19:37), and "smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered" (13:7; Matt 26:31). The Branch who is both priest and king (6:12–13) is Christ.
debated: Unity of the book — one author (traditional) vs. "Second Zechariah" (9–14) by later writers (common critical view), noting the shift in style and setting.

Matthew 27:9 attributes the thirty pieces of silver prophecy to "Jeremy" (Jeremiah); explanations include a combined reference to Jeremiah 19 and 32 with Zechariah 11, or Jeremiah standing at the head of a prophetic scroll.

intros.author: "Malachi" (1:1), which means "my messenger." It is debated whether this is a personal name or a title (cf. 3:1, "I will send my messenger"). The Targum identified the author with Ezra.
intros.date: Probably c. 460–430 BC: the temple has been rebuilt and sacrifices are offered (1:7–10), a Persian governor is in place (1:8), and the abuses (corrupt priests, mixed marriages, neglected tithes) match those Nehemiah confronted (Neh 13).
intros.audience: The post-exilic community in Judah, especially the priests.
intros.setting: About a century after the return: disillusionment, spiritual apathy and cynicism ("Wherein hast thou loved us?" 1:2).
intros.empires: The Persian Empire (Artaxerxes I). Edom's ruin (1:3–4) may reflect Arab/Nabatean encroachment on Edom in the 5th century BC.
intros.genre: Prophetic disputation: a series of exchanges in which God makes a statement, the people object ("Wherein...?"), and God answers.
intros.purpose: To call careless priests and people back to covenant faithfulness and to announce the coming of the Lord to His temple, preceded by His messenger.
intros.themes: God's electing love (1:2); honoring God with pure offerings; the priestly covenant; faithfulness in marriage ("he hateth putting away," 2:16); tithes; the day of the LORD; the Sun of righteousness "with healing in his wings" (4:2); Elijah's coming.
outline: 2:17–3:6 The coming messenger and the Lord's refining
3:13–4:6 The book of remembrance; the day of the LORD; Elijah
intros.christ: Jesus identified John the Baptist as the messenger of 3:1 and as the promised Elijah (4:5; Matt 11:10–14; Mark 9:11–13), making Malachi the bridge between the Testaments. The "Lord, whom ye seek," who "shall suddenly come to his temple" (3:1), is Christ, and He is the "Sun of righteousness."
debated: Whether "Malachi" is a personal name or a title.
Precise date (before Nehemiah's arrival, between his two terms, or after).

intros.author: Anonymous in the text; early church tradition unanimously ascribes it to Matthew (Levi), the tax collector who became an apostle (9:9; 10:3). Papias (early 2nd century, quoted by Eusebius) said Matthew "arranged the oracles in the Hebrew [or Aramaic] language." Many modern scholars doubt apostolic authorship because the Gospel appears to use Mark extensively.
intros.date: Traditional: before AD 70 (some say 50s–60s). Many modern scholars: AD 80–90, after the destruction of Jerusalem, partly because they read 22:7 and 24 as reflecting that event.
intros.audience: Primarily Jewish Christians, probably in Syria (Antioch is often suggested) or Palestine; the Gospel assumes knowledge of Jewish customs and emphasizes fulfillment of the Old Testament.
intros.setting: Jesus' life and ministry in Galilee and Judea, c. 6/4 BC – AD 30/33, under Roman rule through Herod the Great, his sons (Herod Antipas, Archelaus), and Roman prefects (Pontius Pilate).
intros.empires: The Roman Empire (Caesar Augustus, Tiberius), ruling Judea through client kings and prefects; the Jewish high-priestly aristocracy and Sanhedrin held limited authority under Rome.
intros.genre: Gospel: a theological biography of Jesus, organized around five major discourses.
intros.purpose: To show that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of David and Son of Abraham, who fulfills the Law and the Prophets, and to call all nations to become His disciples.
intros.themes: Fulfillment ("that it might be fulfilled"); the kingdom of heaven; Jesus as teacher greater than Moses (Sermon on the Mount, 5–7); righteousness; the Church (16:18; 18); Immanuel, "God with us" (1:23; 28:20); the Great Commission (28:18–20).
outline: 14–17 Jesus and the disciples; Peter's confession
intros.christ: The entire Gospel presents Jesus as the Christ: born of a virgin in Bethlehem, fulfilling prophecy, teaching with authority, giving His life "a ransom for many" (20:28), instituting the Supper "for the remission of sins" (26:28), and rising as the Lord with all authority.
debated: Authorship — the apostle Matthew (early church tradition) vs. an unknown Jewish-Christian author using Mark and a sayings source "Q" (common modern view).
The Synoptic Problem — Markan priority (majority) vs. Matthean priority (Augustine, and the modern "Griesbach/two-Gospel" hypothesis); the existence of Q is also debated.
Date — Traditional: before AD 70. Main critical view: c. AD 80–90.
Papias' "Hebrew" Matthew — its relation to our Greek Gospel is unclear.

intros.author: Anonymous in the text; early tradition (Papias, Irenaeus) ascribes it to John Mark, companion of Paul and Barnabas (Acts 12:12, 25) and later of Peter (1 Pet 5:13), who wrote down Peter's preaching.
intros.date: Probably AD 55–70; many place it in the late 60s, around the Neronian persecution in Rome (64) or the Jewish War (66–70).
intros.audience: Gentile Christians, traditionally in Rome: Mark explains Jewish customs (7:3–4) and Aramaic words, and uses some Latin loanwords.
intros.setting: Jesus' ministry in Galilee and his last week in Jerusalem.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire. If written in Rome under Nero, the readers knew persecution firsthand.
intros.genre: Gospel, fast-paced ("straightway" occurs over 40 times), with a large proportion devoted to the Passion.
intros.purpose: To proclaim "the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God" (1:1) and to show that the Messiah came to suffer, die and rise, calling disciples to take up the cross.
intros.themes: Jesus' authority over demons, disease, nature, and sin; the "messianic secret"; the misunderstanding of the disciples; the suffering Son of Man; "the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many" (10:45); the centurion's confession (15:39).
outline: 8:27–10:52 On the way to Jerusalem: Peter's confession and three Passion predictions
intros.christ: Mark opens and closes with the confession of Jesus as Son of God (1:1, 11; 15:39), and centers on the cross: the Messiah is revealed most fully as the crucified One.
debated: The ending — the oldest Greek manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) end at 16:8; the "longer ending" (16:9–20, printed in the KJV) is found in the great majority of manuscripts and was known by the 2nd century (Irenaeus), but many scholars regard it as a later addition. Whether Mark intended to end at 16:8 or the original ending was lost is also debated.
Peter's influence on Mark (traditional) — accepted, doubted, or modified by modern scholars.
Markan priority (see Matthew).

intros.author: Anonymous in the text; early tradition (the Muratorian fragment, Irenaeus) ascribes it to Luke, "the beloved physician" (Col 4:14) and companion of Paul. The same author wrote Acts (Luke 1:1–4; Acts 1:1), and the "we" passages of Acts (e.g., 16:10–17) suggest he traveled with Paul.
intros.date: Traditional: c. AD 60–62, before Acts, which ends with Paul still awaiting trial in Rome. Many modern scholars: AD 80–90.
intros.audience: "Most excellent Theophilus" (1:3), probably a Gentile of standing, and through him a wider Gentile Christian readership.
intros.setting: From the births of John the Baptist and Jesus to the ascension, with a long "travel narrative" (9:51–19:27) as Jesus journeys to Jerusalem.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire: Luke anchors events in world history (Caesar Augustus' census, 2:1; the fifteenth year of Tiberius, 3:1; Pilate, Herod Antipas, Philip, Lysanias, Annas and Caiaphas).
intros.genre: Gospel written as an orderly historical account in polished Greek, based on eyewitness testimony (1:1–4).
intros.purpose: To give Theophilus "certainty" concerning the things he had been taught (1:4): that Jesus is the Savior of all people, Jew and Gentile.
intros.themes: Salvation ("the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost," 19:10); the Holy Spirit; prayer; joy; concern for the poor, women, Samaritans, outcasts; the canticles (Magnificat, Benedictus, Nunc Dimittis); parables of grace (the prodigal son, the good Samaritan); repentance and forgiveness preached to all nations (24:47).
outline: 1–2 Births and childhood of John and Jesus
intros.christ: Luke presents Jesus as the Savior "which is Christ the Lord" (2:11), the one in whom the Scriptures are fulfilled (4:21; 24:27, 44–47), who forgives the penitent thief (23:43) and opens the Scriptures to show that "Christ ought to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory" (24:26).
debated: Authorship by Luke (widely accepted even by some critical scholars, though others dispute that the author knew Paul personally).
Date — Traditional: early 60s, before Acts, which ends with Paul still awaiting trial (c. AD 62). Main critical view: c. AD 80–90.

The census of Quirinius (2:2) — Josephus dates a census under Quirinius to AD 6, after Herod's death (4 BC); proposed solutions include an earlier census or role of Quirinius, or translating "before" Quirinius was governor; critics see an error.

intros.author: The Gospel names its author as "the disciple whom Jesus loved" (21:20–24), an eyewitness. Early tradition (Irenaeus, who knew Polycarp, a disciple of John) identifies him as the apostle John son of Zebedee, writing in Ephesus. Some ancient and modern scholars attribute it to "John the Elder" (mentioned by Papias) or to a "Johannine community."
intros.date: Traditional: c. AD 85–95. A papyrus fragment of John (P52, Rylands Library) is commonly dated to the early-to-mid 2nd century, ruling out the very late dates once proposed; its precise date is itself debated. Some scholars argue for a date before AD 70.
intros.audience: Christians and seekers, probably in Asia Minor (Ephesus), both Jewish and Gentile.
intros.setting: Jesus' ministry, with more emphasis on Judea and Jerusalem than the Synoptics, structured around several Jewish feasts (three Passovers, implying a ministry of over two years).
intros.empires: The Roman Empire. Late in the 1st century, Christians were increasingly separated from the synagogue (cf. 9:22; 16:2).
intros.genre: Gospel, with long discourses and selected "signs."
intros.purpose: "These are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name" (20:31).
intros.themes: The eternal Word made flesh (1:1, 14); signs; the "I am" sayings (bread of life, light of the world, door, good shepherd, resurrection and life, way-truth-life, true vine; and "Before Abraham was, I am," 8:58); believing; eternal life; the Father and the Son; the Holy Spirit as Comforter (14–16); glory revealed in the cross.
outline: 1:19–12:50 The book of signs: seven signs and discourses
13–17 The upper room: footwashing, farewell discourse, high-priestly prayer
intros.christ: John is explicitly about Christ: the Word who was God, the Lamb of God that takes away the sin of the world (1:29), the giver of new birth by water and the Spirit (3:5), the one lifted up like the serpent (3:14), confessed by Thomas as "My Lord and my God" (20:28). Luther called it "the one, tender, true chief Gospel" (see his Preface to the New Testament).
debated: Authorship — the apostle John (tradition) vs. the Elder John or a later community.
Relationship to the Synoptics and historical value of the discourses.
Chronology of the Last Supper and crucifixion relative to Passover, compared with the Synoptics.

The passage on the woman taken in adultery (7:53–8:11), printed in the KJV, is absent from the earliest manuscripts and regarded by most textual scholars as a later insertion (many accept it as an authentic tradition).

intros.author: Luke, the author of the third Gospel (1:1; see Luke).
intros.date: Traditional: c. AD 62, since the narrative ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome for two years (28:30) without recording his trial outcome or death, Nero's persecution, or Jerusalem's fall. Many modern scholars: AD 80–90; some later.
intros.audience: Theophilus (1:1) and the wider Church.
intros.setting: About 30 years from the ascension (c. AD 30/33) to Paul in Rome (c. AD 60–62): Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, Antioch, Asia Minor, Macedonia, Greece, and Rome.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire: emperors Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius (who expelled Jews from Rome, 18:2), and Nero (the "Caesar" to whom Paul appealed, 25:11); provincial governors such as Gallio (an inscription at Delphi dates his proconsulship to c. AD 51–52, a key anchor for Pauline chronology), Felix and Festus; client kings Herod Agrippa I and II.
intros.genre: Historical narrative (the second volume of Luke-Acts), with speeches and travel accounts.
intros.purpose: To show how the risen Christ, by the Holy Spirit, spread the Gospel "both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth" (1:8), and that the Gentiles are received by faith without the law of Moses.
intros.themes: The Holy Spirit (Pentecost); witness to the resurrection; the Word growing (6:7; 12:24; 19:20); Baptism and repentance; the Church's life together; persecution; the inclusion of Gentiles (10–11; 15); Paul's missionary journeys; God's providence bringing the Gospel to Rome.
outline: 8–12 Witness in Judea and Samaria; Saul's conversion; Cornelius; the church at Antioch
21:17–28:31 Paul's arrest, trials, voyage, and Rome
intros.christ: Acts is the continuation of "all that Jesus began both to do and teach" (1:1): the ascended Lord pours out the Spirit, and the apostles preach Christ crucified and risen from the Scriptures (2:22–36; 8:35; 13:26–39). "Neither is there salvation in any other" (4:12).
debated: Historical reliability — high (Luke's accurate use of local titles of officials, e.g., "politarchs" at Thessalonica, is frequently noted) vs. theological idealization; the relationship between Acts and Paul's letters (e.g., Galatians 2 and Acts 15).

Date — Traditional: c. AD 62, since Acts ends with Paul still awaiting trial and does not mention his death, Nero's persecution, or Jerusalem's fall. Main critical view: c. AD 80–90 (a minority places it in the early 2nd century).
The "Western" text of Acts, about 8 percent longer than other manuscripts.

intros.author: The apostle Paul (1:1), dictated to Tertius (16:22). Pauline authorship is almost universally accepted.
intros.date: c. AD 57, from Corinth, near the end of Paul's third missionary journey, before he took the collection to Jerusalem (15:25–26; Acts 20:2–3).
intros.audience: The Christians in Rome, a church Paul had not founded or yet visited, made up of Jewish and Gentile believers (with Gentiles probably the majority).
intros.setting: Claudius had expelled Jews from Rome c. AD 49 (Acts 18:2); after his death (AD 54) many returned, possibly causing tension between Jewish and Gentile Christians (14–15). Paul hoped to visit Rome on his way to Spain (15:24, 28).
intros.empires: The Roman Empire under Nero (in the early, relatively stable years of his reign). Romans 13 addresses the Christian's relationship to governing authorities.
intros.genre: Letter; the most systematic of Paul's epistles, using diatribe (questions and answers with an imagined objector).
intros.purpose: To set forth the Gospel Paul preached — the righteousness of God revealed through faith — to unite Jewish and Gentile believers, and to win the Romans' support for his mission to Spain.
intros.themes: The Gospel as the power of God unto salvation (1:16–17); universal sin under the Law (1:18–3:20); justification by grace through faith apart from works of the law (3:21–4:25); Adam and Christ (5); Baptism and new life (6); the Law and the struggle with sin (7); life in the Spirit; nothing can separate us from God's love (8); Israel and God's mercy (9–11); living sacrifices (12); love fulfilling the law (13).
outline: 1:18–3:20 The wrath of God: all have sinned
6–8 New life in Christ and the Spirit
intros.christ: Christ is the content of the Gospel (1:3–4): "set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood" (3:25), "delivered for our offences, and raised again for our justification" (4:25), "the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth" (10:4). Luther's Preface calls Romans "really the chief part of the New Testament and the very purest Gospel."
debated: Romans 7:14–25 — Paul as a believer struggling with sin (Augustine, Luther: the Christian is "simul iustus et peccator") vs. Paul describing life under the law before or apart from Christ.
Chapter 16 — part of the original letter (majority view) or a note sent elsewhere (e.g., to Ephesus).

"Works of the law" and "righteousness of God" — debated in the "New Perspective on Paul" (Sanders, Dunn, Wright), which reads them mainly as Jewish boundary markers; Lutheran theology maintains that Paul excludes all human works from justification.
Romans 9–11 and the meaning of "all Israel shall be saved" (11:26).

intros.author: The apostle Paul, with Sosthenes (1:1). Pauline authorship is universally accepted.
intros.date: c. AD 53–55, from Ephesus (16:8) during Paul's third journey.
intros.audience: The church at Corinth, which Paul founded c. AD 50–51 (Acts 18), mostly Gentile with some Jewish members.
intros.setting: Corinth, refounded as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar in 44 BC, was a wealthy, cosmopolitan commercial city on the isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, capital of the province of Achaia, known for its temples, the Isthmian games, and loose morals. The church was troubled by factions, immorality, lawsuits, questions about marriage, food offered to idols, worship, spiritual gifts, and the resurrection. Paul answers reports from "Chloe's people" (1:11) and a letter from the Corinthians (7:1).
intros.empires: The Roman Empire (Claudius, then Nero); Corinth was a showcase of Roman culture in Greece.
intros.genre: Pastoral letter addressing specific problems.
intros.purpose: To correct divisions and disorders and to ground every issue in the Gospel of Christ crucified and risen.
intros.themes: The word of the cross, foolishness to the world and the power of God (1:18–25); the unity of the body of Christ; holiness and church discipline (5); Christian freedom limited by love (8–10); the Lord's Supper (10:16–17; 11:23–29); spiritual gifts; love (13); the resurrection of Christ and of the dead (15).
outline: 8–10 Food sacrificed to idols; Christian freedom
11–14 Worship: head coverings, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts, love
intros.christ: "I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified" (2:2). Christ is "made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption" (1:30), "our passover" (5:7), present in His body and blood in the Supper (10:16; 11:24–25), and "the firstfruits of them that slept" (15:20).
debated: Head coverings and women's silence (11:2–16; 14:33–35) — interpreted variously; some critics argue 14:34–35 is a later insertion; confessional Lutheran churches have generally read these passages, with 1 Timothy 2, as bearing on the pastoral office.
The meaning of "baptism for the dead" (15:29), which has no agreed explanation.
Number of letters — 1 Cor 5:9 mentions an earlier letter, now lost.

intros.author: The apostle Paul, with Timothy (1:1).
intros.date: c. AD 55–56, from Macedonia (2:13; 7:5), some months after 1 Corinthians.
intros.audience: The church at Corinth and the believers throughout Achaia (1:1).
intros.setting: Between the two letters, Paul had made a "painful visit" (2:1) and written a "severe letter" with tears (2:4). Titus brought news that most of the church had repented (7:6–16), but "super-apostles" (11:5) were attacking Paul's authority.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire; see 1 Corinthians.
intros.genre: Personal and pastoral letter, the most autobiographical of Paul's epistles.
intros.purpose: To express joy at the church's repentance, to defend the character of Paul's apostolic ministry, to encourage the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, and to warn against false apostles.
intros.themes: The God of all comfort (1:3–4); the ministry of the new covenant and the Spirit (3); treasure in earthen vessels (4:7); the ministry of reconciliation ("God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself," 5:19); generous giving (8–9); strength in weakness ("my grace is sufficient for thee," 12:9).
outline: 1–7 Paul's ministry explained: comfort, reconciliation, joy
10–13 Defense against false apostles; Paul's "boasting" in weakness
intros.christ: "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him" (5:21) — the "joyful exchange" central to Luther's theology. "Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor" (8:9).
debated: Unity — one letter (traditional) vs. a compilation of two or more letters (many critics see chapters 10–13 as part of the "severe letter," and 6:14–7:1 as an insertion).
Identity of Paul's opponents and of the "thorn in the flesh" (12:7).

intros.author: The apostle Paul (1:1). Universally accepted.
intros.date: Depends on the destination: c. AD 48–49 (before the Jerusalem Council; "South Galatia" view), or c. AD 53–57 ("North Galatia" view).
intros.audience: "The churches of Galatia" (1:2): either the cities of the southern part of the Roman province (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe, evangelized on the first journey, Acts 13–14) or ethnic Galatians (Celts) in the north-central region.
intros.setting: After Paul left, teachers (often called "Judaizers") insisted that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be full members of God's people, and questioned Paul's apostleship.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire; Galatia became a Roman province in 25 BC.
intros.genre: Polemical letter, urgent in tone (no thanksgiving section).
intros.purpose: To defend the Gospel of justification by faith in Christ apart from the works of the law and to call the Galatians to stand fast in Christian freedom.
intros.themes: One Gospel (1:6–9); Paul's apostleship from Christ; justification by faith ("a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ," 2:16); Abraham's faith; the purpose of the Law as a "schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ" (3:24); adoption; freedom; the fruit of the Spirit (5:22–23); bearing one another's burdens.
outline: 1–2 Paul's Gospel is from God: autobiography; rebuke of Peter at Antioch
3–4 Justification by faith: Abraham, the Law, sons and heirs, Hagar and Sarah
5–6 Freedom in the Spirit: love, fruit, bearing burdens
intros.christ: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me... the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me" (2:20). "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us" (3:13). In his Table Talk Luther likened his attachment to Galatians to his marriage with Katharina von Bora.
debated: North vs. South Galatia and the resulting date; relation of Galatians 2:1–10 to Acts 11 (famine visit) or Acts 15 (Council).
"Faith of Jesus Christ" (2:16; Greek pistis Christou) — faith in Christ (traditional) vs. the faithfulness of Christ (some recent scholars).
New Perspective debates about "works of the law" (see Romans).

intros.author: The apostle Paul (1:1; 3:1), writing as a prisoner. Many critical scholars regard Ephesians as written by a later follower of Paul (deutero-Pauline), citing differences in style and vocabulary and its close relationship to Colossians.
intros.date: If Pauline, c. AD 60–62, during his Roman imprisonment (some propose Ephesus or Caesarea). If pseudonymous, c. AD 80–90.
intros.audience: "The saints which are at Ephesus" (1:1); the words "at Ephesus" are missing in some of the earliest manuscripts (P46, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus), and the letter lacks personal greetings, so many think it was a circular letter to churches in Asia Minor, including Ephesus.
intros.setting: Ephesus, capital of the province of Asia, a great port and home of the temple of Artemis (Diana), one of the seven wonders of the ancient world; Paul spent nearly three years there (Acts 19; 20:31).
intros.empires: The Roman Empire. The background includes widespread fear of spiritual "principalities and powers," magic (Acts 19:19), and the imperial cult.
intros.genre: Letter, with long doctrinal prayers and blessings (1–3) followed by exhortation (4–6).
intros.purpose: To unfold God's eternal plan to unite all things in Christ and to make one new people of Jews and Gentiles, and to call the Church to live worthily of that calling.
intros.themes: Every spiritual blessing in Christ; election and predestination in Christ (1:4–5); salvation by grace through faith, not of works (2:8–9); the Church as Christ's body, temple, and bride; unity of Jew and Gentile; the gifts of ministry (4:11–12); Christian households (5:21–6:9); the armor of God (6:10–18).
outline: 2 Saved by grace; one new man
intros.christ: God's plan is "to gather together in one all things in Christ" (1:10). Christ "is our peace," breaking down the dividing wall (2:14). His love for the Church, for which He gave Himself "that he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word" (5:25–26), is the model for marriage.
debated: Authorship — Paul (traditional, still held by many scholars) vs. a later disciple (widely held in critical scholarship).

Destination — the words "at Ephesus" (1:1) are missing from some of the earliest manuscripts, so many think the letter was a circular letter for several churches of Asia (possibly the "epistle from Laodicea," Col 4:16).
Relationship to Colossians — Traditional: written by Paul at the same time and carried by the same messenger, Tychicus (Eph 6:21; Col 4:7). Critical: a later writer used Colossians as a model.

intros.author: The apostle Paul, with Timothy (1:1). Universally accepted.
intros.date: During an imprisonment (1:7, 13): traditionally Rome, c. AD 61–62 (note "Caesar's household," 4:22, and the "praetorium," 1:13). Some propose Ephesus (c. AD 54–55) or Caesarea (c. AD 57–59).
intros.audience: The church at Philippi, the first church Paul founded in Europe (Acts 16), with whom he had an especially warm relationship.
intros.setting: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, settled by veterans after the battle of Philippi (42 BC); its citizens were proud of their Roman citizenship (cf. 3:20, "our conversation [citizenship] is in heaven"). The Philippians had sent Epaphroditus with a gift (4:18).
intros.empires: The Roman Empire under Nero.
intros.genre: Letter of friendship and thanks.
intros.purpose: To thank the Philippians for their gift, to report on Paul's circumstances, to encourage unity and humility, and to warn against false teachers.
intros.themes: Joy ("Rejoice in the Lord alway," 4:4); partnership in the Gospel; to live is Christ (1:21); the humility and exaltation of Christ (2:5–11); righteousness through faith, not of the law (3:9); contentment (4:11–13); peace (4:7).
outline: 1 Thanksgiving; Paul's imprisonment advances the Gospel
2 The mind of Christ; Timothy and Epaphroditus
3 Warning against confidence in the flesh; pressing on
intros.christ: The great "Christ hymn" (2:5–11) confesses Christ, "being in the form of God," who "made himself of no reputation... and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross," and whom God exalted with "a name which is above every name."
debated: Place and date of imprisonment (Rome vs. Ephesus vs. Caesarea).
Unity — one letter (majority) vs. a compilation (because of the abrupt shift at 3:1–2).
Whether 2:6–11 is a pre-Pauline hymn quoted by Paul.

intros.author: The apostle Paul, with Timothy (1:1). Some critical scholars regard it as deutero-Pauline because of differences in style and theology; many accept it as Paul's.
intros.date: If Pauline, during an imprisonment, traditionally Rome c. AD 60–62, sent together with Philemon and probably Ephesians by Tychicus (4:7–9).
intros.audience: The church at Colossae, a town in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor near Laodicea and Hierapolis, founded not by Paul but by Epaphras (1:7).
intros.setting: A false teaching (the "Colossian heresy") combined philosophy, ascetic regulations, observance of special days, and the worship of angels (2:8, 16–23), apparently diminishing Christ. Colossae was damaged by an earthquake c. AD 60–61 (reported by Tacitus for nearby Laodicea).
intros.empires: The Roman Empire.
intros.genre: Letter.
intros.purpose: To show the supremacy and sufficiency of Christ against a teaching that added to Him, and to call the believers to live the new life they have in Him.
intros.themes: The preeminence of Christ (1:15–20); "in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily" (2:9); complete in Christ; Baptism as burial and resurrection with Christ (2:11–12); freedom from human regulations; setting minds on things above (3:1–4); household instructions.
outline: 1:15–2:5 The supremacy of Christ; Paul's ministry
intros.christ: Christ is "the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: for by him were all things created... and by him all things consist," and "he is the head of the body, the church" (1:15–18). He "blotted out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us... nailing it to his cross" (2:14).
debated: Authorship — Traditional: Paul (1:1; 4:18), accepted by many modern scholars too. Main critical view: divided; a substantial number regard it as written by a follower of Paul.
The exact nature of the Colossian heresy (Jewish mysticism, early Gnostic ideas, local folk religion, or a mixture).

intros.author: Paul, with Silvanus (Silas) and Timothy (1:1). Universally accepted.
intros.date: c. AD 50–51, from Corinth, shortly after Paul's hurried departure from Thessalonica (Acts 17:1–10; 18:5). Probably one of Paul's earliest letters (if Galatians is not earlier).
intros.audience: The young church at Thessalonica, largely Gentile converts who "turned to God from idols" (1:9).
intros.setting: Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia and a free city on the Via Egnatia. The new believers faced persecution, and some were grieving members who had died before Christ's return.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire under Claudius. The charge against the believers was acting "contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, one Jesus" (Acts 17:7).
intros.genre: Pastoral letter.
intros.purpose: To encourage the persecuted believers, defend Paul's conduct, exhort them to holiness and brotherly love, and comfort them concerning the dead in Christ and the Lord's coming.
intros.themes: Faith, love and hope (1:3); the Word received as the word of God (2:13); holiness and sexual purity (4:3–8); the resurrection of believers at Christ's return (4:13–18); the day of the Lord as a thief in the night (5:2); watchfulness.
outline: 2–3 Paul's ministry and concern for them
intros.christ: "Jesus, which delivered us from the wrath to come" (1:10); "God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation by our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us" (5:9–10); the returning Lord will raise the dead in Christ.
debated: Whether 2:14–16 (on the Jews who killed the Lord) is original (majority) or a later insertion (some critics).

Interpretation of 4:17 ("caught up") — the Church's meeting with the returning Lord at the visible last day (historic Lutheran and most interpreters) vs. a secret pre-tribulation "rapture" (dispensationalism).

intros.author: Paul, with Silvanus and Timothy (1:1), with his own signature (3:17). Many critical scholars regard it as pseudonymous, citing differences in eschatology from 1 Thessalonians; others accept Pauline authorship.
intros.date: If Pauline, a few months after 1 Thessalonians, c. AD 51, from Corinth.
intros.audience: The church at Thessalonica.
intros.setting: Persecution continued; some had been unsettled by a claim, perhaps in a forged letter, that "the day of Christ is at hand" (2:2), and some were refusing to work.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire. Interpreters have often linked "he who now letteth" (restrains, 2:7) with the Roman order of the time.
intros.genre: Pastoral letter.
intros.purpose: To encourage the persecuted, to correct the idea that the day of the Lord had already come, and to command the idle to work.
intros.themes: God's righteous judgment at Christ's revelation (1:5–10); the man of sin and the falling away that must come first (2:3–12); standing fast in the traditions taught (2:15); "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (3:10).
outline: 2 The day of the Lord and the man of sin
3 Prayer request and warning against idleness
intros.christ: The Lord Jesus will be "revealed from heaven with his mighty angels" (1:7) and will destroy the lawless one "with the spirit of his mouth, and... with the brightness of his coming" (2:8).
debated: Authorship — Traditional: Paul, shortly after 1 Thessalonians. Main critical view: divided; many consider it a later imitation because of its different picture of the end.

Identity of the "man of sin" and the "restrainer" — the Lutheran Confessions identify the Antichrist of 2:3–4 with the papacy as an institution (Smalcald Articles II.4; Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope); other interpretations include a single future individual, a past Roman figure, or a recurring principle.

intros.author: The apostle Paul (1:1). 1–2 Timothy and Titus (the "Pastoral Epistles") are widely regarded by critical scholars as written by a later follower of Paul (c. AD 90–120), citing differences in vocabulary, church organization, and the difficulty of fitting them into Acts. Traditional scholars defend Pauline authorship, often suggesting Paul used a secretary and was released from his first Roman imprisonment before a later arrest.
intros.date: If Pauline, c. AD 62–64, after Paul's release from his first Roman imprisonment, from Macedonia (1:3).
intros.audience: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker and "own son in the faith" (1:2), left in Ephesus to oversee the church; and through him the congregation.
intros.setting: False teachers in Ephesus promoted myths, endless genealogies, speculative uses of the law, and asceticism (forbidding marriage and foods, 4:3).
intros.empires: The Roman Empire under Nero; Christians are to pray "for kings, and for all that are in authority" (2:2).
intros.genre: Pastoral letter of instruction.
intros.purpose: To instruct Timothy how people "ought to behave... in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth" (3:15): sound doctrine, public prayer, qualifications for overseers and deacons, care of widows, and warnings about false teaching and the love of money.
intros.themes: Sound doctrine; the proper use of the law (1:8–11); "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief" (1:15); one Mediator (2:5); qualifications for bishops and deacons (3); godliness with contentment (6:6); "the love of money is the root of all evil" (6:10); the good fight of faith.
outline: 1 Warning against false teachers; Paul's testimony
3 Overseers and deacons; the mystery of godliness
intros.christ: "There is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; who gave himself a ransom for all" (2:5–6). "God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit... received up into glory" (3:16).
debated: Authorship of the Pastoral Epistles — Traditional: Paul, after a release from his first Roman imprisonment. Main critical view: a later follower writing in Paul's name (c. AD 90–120), citing vocabulary, church order, and the difficulty of fitting the letters into Acts.
Church offices — the relationship of "bishop" and "elder" (presbyter), and the role of women in public worship (2:11–15), are interpreted in different ways among churches.

intros.author: The apostle Paul (1:1); see 1 Timothy on the debate regarding the Pastoral Epistles.
intros.date: If Pauline, c. AD 64–67, during a second, harsher Roman imprisonment shortly before Paul's martyrdom under Nero ("the time of my departure is at hand," 4:6).
intros.audience: Timothy, apparently still in or near Ephesus.
intros.setting: Paul is chained in Rome (1:16–17), deserted by many, with only Luke with him (4:11), and expecting death. Nero's persecution followed the fire of Rome (AD 64).
intros.empires: The Roman Empire under Nero; tradition holds that Paul was beheaded in Rome.
intros.genre: Personal letter; Paul's last testament.
intros.purpose: To encourage Timothy to be strong, to guard the Gospel, to endure suffering, to preach the Word, and to come to Paul quickly.
intros.themes: Guard the good deposit (1:14); suffering for the Gospel; the faithful Word ("rightly dividing the word of truth," 2:15); perilous last days; the inspiration and sufficiency of Scripture ("All scripture is given by inspiration of God," 3:16–17); "Preach the word" (4:2); the crown of righteousness.
outline: 3 Perilous times; the sufficiency of Scripture
intros.christ: "Our Saviour Jesus Christ... hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel" (1:10). "Remember that Jesus Christ of the seed of David was raised from the dead" (2:8). The Lord, "the righteous judge," will give the crown to all who love His appearing (4:8).
debated: Authorship (see 1 Timothy); some scholars who doubt 1 Timothy and Titus think 2 Timothy contains genuine Pauline fragments.
Whether Paul had a second Roman imprisonment (supported by early tradition, e.g., 1 Clement and Eusebius; doubted by others).

intros.author: The apostle Paul (1:1); see 1 Timothy on the debate regarding the Pastoral Epistles.
intros.date: If Pauline, c. AD 62–64, between 1 and 2 Timothy, after a mission to Crete not recorded in Acts.
intros.audience: Titus, a Gentile co-worker (Gal 2:3), left in Crete to "set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city" (1:5).
intros.setting: The churches of Crete, an island with a poor reputation ("The Cretians are alway liars," 1:12, quoting the Cretan poet Epimenides), troubled by teachers "of the circumcision" spreading Jewish myths.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire; Crete was part of the joint province of Crete and Cyrene.
intros.genre: Pastoral letter of instruction.
intros.purpose: To instruct Titus to appoint qualified elders, to silence false teachers, and to teach sound doctrine that produces godly living in every group of the church.
intros.themes: Qualified elders (1:5–9); sound doctrine and good works; the grace of God that brings salvation and teaches godliness (2:11–14); "not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost" (3:5).
outline: 2 Sound doctrine for every group; the grace of God
3 Good citizenship; saved by mercy; final instructions
intros.christ: Believers look for "the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ; who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity" (2:13–14). Salvation comes through Baptism, poured out "abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour" (3:6).
debated: Authorship — Traditional: Paul. Main critical view: a later follower (see 1 Timothy).
Whether 2:13 calls Jesus "God" directly ("our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ") — the grammatically favored reading of most scholars — or distinguishes God and the Savior.

intros.author: Paul, with Timothy (1). Universally accepted.
intros.date: c. AD 60–62, during Paul's imprisonment (traditionally in Rome), sent with Colossians (Col 4:7–9; Onesimus is mentioned in both).
intros.audience: Philemon, a well-to-do Christian in Colossae in whose house a church met, with Apphia, Archippus, and the church (1–2).
intros.setting: Onesimus, Philemon's slave, had run away (or perhaps sought Paul out as a mediator after a quarrel) and had become a Christian through Paul. Paul sends him back with this letter.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire, in which slavery was pervasive and runaway slaves faced severe punishment.
intros.genre: Short personal letter of appeal (25 verses).
intros.purpose: To appeal to Philemon to receive Onesimus back "not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved" (16), and to forgive him, charging any debt to Paul's account.
intros.themes: Christian love and reconciliation; brotherhood in Christ transcending social status; intercession; "useful" (Onesimus means "useful," v. 11 plays on the name).
outline: 1–7 Greeting and thanksgiving for Philemon's love
intros.christ: Luther's Preface to Philemon puts it this way: "What Christ has done for us with God the Father, that St. Paul does for Onesimus with Philemon" and "we are all his Onesimi, if we believe" (Works of Martin Luther, Philadelphia ed., vol. 6, 1932, p. 473). Paul's offer, "put that on mine account" (18), pictures Christ's substitution for sinners.
debated: Onesimus' situation — a fugitive slave (traditional) vs. a slave seeking an advocate, or sent by Philemon to serve Paul.
Whether Paul hinted that Philemon should free Onesimus (21), and the letter's significance for the later Christian rejection of slavery.

intros.author: Anonymous. Eastern tradition (Clement and Origen of Alexandria) linked it with Paul, though Origen famously said "who wrote the epistle, in truth God knows." Tertullian suggested Barnabas; Luther proposed Apollos; others suggest Luke, Silas, or Priscilla. The style is unlike Paul's, and the author says he received the Gospel through others (2:3). Its canonical acceptance in the West was slow, partly because of uncertainty about authorship.
intros.date: Probably before AD 70: the Levitical sacrifices are spoken of as still being offered (8:4; 10:1–2), and the destruction of the temple, which would have strengthened the argument, is not mentioned. Clement of Rome quotes it c. AD 95–96.
intros.audience: "The Hebrews": Jewish Christians, perhaps in Rome ("They of Italy salute you," 13:24), tempted under persecution to drift back to Judaism.
intros.setting: The readers had endured earlier persecution (10:32–34) and now faced pressure that could lead to apostasy. Timothy had been released from prison (13:23).
intros.empires: The Roman Empire. If the audience was in Rome, Claudius' expulsion (AD 49) and Nero's persecution (AD 64) may be in view.
intros.genre: A "word of exhortation" (13:22): a sermon in written form with a letter-ending, alternating doctrinal exposition and warnings.
intros.purpose: To show the superiority of Christ and the new covenant over the angels, Moses, Aaron's priesthood and the Levitical sacrifices, and to exhort the readers to persevere in faith.
intros.themes: Christ superior to angels and Moses; Christ our High Priest after the order of Melchizedek (5–7); the new covenant (8); the once-for-all sacrifice (9–10); warnings against falling away (2:1–4; 6:4–8; 10:26–31); faith (11); enduring discipline (12); "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (13:8).
outline: 3–4 Superior to Moses; the Sabbath rest
5–7 The great High Priest after Melchizedek
10:19–12:29 Persevere: the hall of faith; running the race
intros.christ: Hebrews is wholly about Christ: the Son "the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person" (1:3), the merciful High Priest tempted like us "yet without sin" (4:15), who "by one offering... hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified" (10:14), "the author and finisher of our faith" (12:2).
debated: Authorship — Older Western and medieval tradition (and the KJV title): Paul. Early Eastern and modern view, both conservative and critical: not Paul; the author is unknown (Apollos, Luther's suggestion; Barnabas; Luke; and others are proposed).
Recipients and location.

The warning passages (6:4–6; 10:26) — whether those who were truly regenerate can fall away (Lutheran teaching holds that believers can fall from grace but also that the penitent are always received) and whether "impossible to renew them again unto repentance" denies restoration; Luther's Preface discusses this difficulty.

intros.author: "James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" (1:1), traditionally James the brother of the Lord, leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13; Gal 1:19), martyred c. AD 62. Some attribute it to a later writer using his name, citing its polished Greek.
intros.date: If by James the Lord's brother, before AD 62; some date it very early (mid-40s), before the Jerusalem Council, making it possibly the earliest New Testament writing.
intros.audience: "The twelve tribes which are scattered abroad" (1:1): Jewish Christians outside Palestine.
intros.setting: Believers facing trials, poverty, and oppression by the rich, with tensions over favoritism, the tongue, and a faith that does not issue in deeds.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire; the oppressing rich (5:1–6) reflect economic inequality in the eastern provinces.
intros.genre: Wisdom-style letter of moral exhortation, resembling Jewish wisdom literature and the Sermon on the Mount.
intros.purpose: To exhort believers to a living faith shown in endurance, wisdom, impartial love, controlled speech, humility, patience, and prayer.
intros.themes: Trials and endurance; wisdom from above; "be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only" (1:22); partiality; faith and works (2:14–26); the tongue (3); humility before God; patience until the Lord's coming; the prayer of faith and anointing of the sick (5:13–18).
outline: 2 Partiality; faith without works is dead
3 The tongue; two kinds of wisdom
5 Warning to the rich; patience; prayer
intros.christ: Christ is named only twice (1:1; 2:1, "the Lord of glory"), but the letter echoes His teaching throughout (e.g., 5:12; Matt 5:34–37) and points to "the coming of the Lord" (5:7–8). Luther, who tested every book by whether it teaches Christ ("What does not teach Christ is not apostolic," his Preface says), found it weak in this respect.
debated: Authorship — Traditional: James the Lord's brother, leader of the Jerusalem church (died c. AD 62). Main critical view: a later writer using his name, citing the polished Greek.

Faith and works: James 2:24 ("by works a man is justified, and not by faith only") and Paul's Romans 3:28 — Luther's Prefaces (1522; softened in later editions) judged James to contradict Paul and placed it near the end of his New Testament, calling it in 1522 "really an epistle of straw" compared to the chief books; the Lutheran Confessions (Apology IV) harmonize the two, teaching that James speaks of the works that show faith is living, not of works that merit justification before God. Most interpreters harmonize similarly.
Canonicity — James was among the "disputed" (antilegomena) books in the early church (Eusebius).

intros.author: The apostle Peter (1:1), written "by Silvanus" (5:12), who may have served as secretary. Some critical scholars doubt Petrine authorship, citing the fine Greek and possible references to widespread persecution later than Peter's lifetime.
intros.date: If by Peter, c. AD 62–64, from "Babylon" (5:13), commonly understood as a cryptic name for Rome, shortly before or at the beginning of Nero's persecution. Others date it to AD 70–90.
intros.audience: "The strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia" (1:1): churches in Asia Minor, largely Gentile (1:14, 18; 4:3).
intros.setting: Believers suffering social hostility, slander, and persecution for their faith.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire; "Honour the king" (2:17) — written under Nero.
intros.genre: Letter of encouragement and exhortation.
intros.purpose: To encourage suffering Christians to stand firm in the true grace of God, living holy lives as God's people in a hostile world, following Christ's example.
intros.themes: A living hope through the resurrection (1:3); rejoicing in trials; holiness; the royal priesthood of all believers (2:9); submission and good conduct; suffering for righteousness; Christ's descent and proclamation to the spirits in prison (3:18–20); Baptism that "doth also now save us" (3:21); humility; the devil "as a roaring lion" (5:8).
outline: 1:1–2:10 The new people of God: salvation, holiness, living stones
2:11–4:11 Living as strangers: submission, suffering, Christ's example
4:12–5:14 Suffering and glory; elders and flock; final greetings
intros.christ: Christ "his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree... by whose stripes ye were healed" (2:24, quoting Isaiah 53); "Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God" (3:18). He is the chief cornerstone and the chief Shepherd.
debated: Authorship — Traditional: the apostle Peter, writing through Silvanus (5:12). Main critical view: a later disciple writing in Peter's name (c. AD 70–100).

Christ preaching to "the spirits in prison" (3:19) — Christ's descent into hell to proclaim His victory (Formula of Concord, Article IX; Luther's Torgau sermon), preaching through Noah in Noah's day, or other views.
"Babylon" = Rome (majority) vs. literal Babylon.

intros.author: "Simon Peter, a servant and an apostle of Jesus Christ" (1:1), who claims to have witnessed the Transfiguration (1:16–18) and refers to this as his second letter (3:1). Many scholars (including some conservatives) consider it pseudonymous, citing differences in style from 1 Peter, its relationship to Jude, and the reference to Paul's letters as "scriptures" (3:16). It was among the most disputed books in the early church (Eusebius).
intros.date: If by Peter, c. AD 64–68, shortly before his death (1:14). If pseudonymous, c. AD 80–130.
intros.audience: The same readers as 1 Peter (3:1), or Christians generally.
intros.setting: False teachers were denying the Lord's return and promoting moral license (2; 3:3–4).
intros.empires: The Roman Empire under Nero (traditional dating).
intros.genre: Letter and farewell testament.
intros.purpose: To urge growth in grace and knowledge, to warn against false teachers, and to affirm the certainty of Christ's return and the day of the Lord.
intros.themes: Growth in Christian virtue (1:5–11); the reliability of apostolic witness and prophetic Scripture ("holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost," 1:21); false teachers and their judgment; scoffers; God's patience ("not willing that any should perish," 3:9); new heavens and new earth (3:13).
outline: 1 Growth in grace; the sure word of prophecy
3 The day of the Lord; final exhortation
intros.christ: The letter begins with "the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ" (1:1) and ends "grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ" (3:18). The Transfiguration witness confirms Him as God's beloved Son.
debated: Authorship — Peter (traditional) vs. pseudonymous (common critical view and some conservatives).
Relationship to Jude (2 Peter 2 closely parallels Jude 4–18; which used which is debated).
Canonicity was debated in the early church; it is among the antilegomena.

intros.author: Anonymous, but the style and vocabulary are very close to John's Gospel; tradition ascribes it to the apostle John. The author claims to be an eyewitness ("that which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes... and our hands have handled," 1:1).
intros.date: c. AD 85–95, probably from Ephesus.
intros.audience: Churches (probably in Asia Minor) known to the author, addressed as "little children."
intros.setting: A group had left the community (2:19) teaching that Jesus Christ had not truly come in the flesh (4:2–3) — perhaps an early form of Docetism or the teaching of Cerinthus — and claiming sinlessness and fellowship with God while disregarding love and obedience.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire under Domitian (if dated in the 90s).
intros.genre: A pastoral tract or sermon (lacking a letter's opening and closing).
intros.purpose: To give assurance of eternal life ("These things have I written unto you that believe... that ye may know that ye have eternal life," 5:13) and to guard against false teaching about Christ.
intros.themes: Fellowship with God; walking in the light; confession of sin and forgiveness ("If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us," 1:9); Christ the propitiation; "God is love" (4:8); testing the spirits; the incarnation; assurance.
outline: 2:28–3:24 Children of God; love one another
4:7–5:12 God is love; faith overcomes the world
intros.christ: "We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous: and he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world" (2:1–2). "The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin" (1:7).
debated: Authorship (apostle John, John the Elder, or a member of a Johannine school).
Identity of the opponents.

The "Johannine Comma" (5:7–8, "in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one"), printed in the KJV, is absent from nearly all Greek manuscripts before the late Middle Ages and from early church writers; most textual scholars regard it as a later addition (Luther did not include it in his translation).

intros.author: "The elder" (1). Tradition identifies him with the apostle John; others with "John the Elder" mentioned by Papias.
intros.date: c. AD 85–95, probably close to 1 John.
intros.audience: "The elect lady and her children" (1), most likely a personified local church and its members, though some take it as an individual woman.
intros.setting: Itinerant false teachers who deny "that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh" (7) were seeking hospitality from the churches.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire.
intros.genre: Short personal letter (13 verses).
intros.purpose: To urge love and obedience, and to warn against receiving and supporting deceivers who deny the incarnation.
intros.themes: Truth and love; walking in the commandments; the deceiver and antichrist; abiding in the doctrine of Christ (9); not giving hospitality to false teachers (10–11).
intros.christ: The letter turns on confessing "that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh" (7); "whosoever... abideth not in the doctrine of Christ, hath not God" (9).
debated: Identity of "the elder" — Traditional: the apostle John. Alternative: "John the Elder," a distinct figure mentioned by Papias.
Whether "the elect lady" is a church or an individual.

intros.author: "The elder" (1); see 2 John.
intros.audience: Gaius, a beloved church member (perhaps not one of the other men named Gaius in the New Testament).
intros.setting: Diotrephes, who "loveth to have the preeminence," was refusing to receive traveling missionaries sent by the elder and expelling those who did. Demetrius, probably the letter carrier, is commended.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire.
intros.genre: Short personal letter (the shortest book of the New Testament by word count).
intros.purpose: To commend Gaius for his hospitality to missionaries, to rebuke Diotrephes, and to commend Demetrius.
intros.themes: Walking in the truth; hospitality as fellowship in the Gospel ("fellowhelpers to the truth," 8); humility versus love of preeminence; imitating good.
outline: 1–4 Greeting and joy in Gaius' faithfulness
intros.christ: The missionaries went out "for his name's sake" (7) — the name of Christ — taking nothing from the Gentiles; supporting them is sharing in the work of the truth.
debated: Identity of the elder; nature of Diotrephes' authority (an early local bishop resisting outside authority, or simply a domineering member).

intros.author: "Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James" (1), traditionally Judas the brother of the Lord (Matt 13:55). Some scholars consider it pseudonymous. It was among the disputed books in the early church, partly because it cites 1 Enoch (14–15) and alludes to a tradition about Michael and the body of Moses (9, probably from the Assumption of Moses).
intros.date: Uncertain; c. AD 65–80 is commonly proposed. Its relationship to 2 Peter affects dating.
intros.audience: Christians (perhaps Jewish Christians) threatened by intruders.
intros.setting: Ungodly men had "crept in unawares," turning grace into licentiousness and denying the Lord (4).
intros.empires: The Roman Empire.
intros.genre: Short letter of warning (25 verses).
intros.purpose: To urge believers to "earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints" (3) and to warn of the judgment of false teachers.
intros.themes: Contending for the faith; examples of judgment (Israel in the wilderness, fallen angels, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam, Korah); building up in faith and prayer; mercy toward the wavering; the great doxology ("Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling," 24–25).
outline: 5–16 Examples of judgment and description of the false teachers
intros.christ: Believers are "preserved in Jesus Christ" (1) and look "for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life" (21); glory belongs to "the only wise God our Saviour... through Jesus Christ our Lord" (25, in modern critical texts).
debated: Authorship and date — Traditional: Jude the brother of James and of the Lord, before c. AD 80. Main critical view: pseudonymous, late 1st or early 2nd century.
Use of non-canonical writings (1 Enoch; Assumption of Moses) — quoting a true statement does not endorse the whole book (common view).
Relationship to 2 Peter 2.
Canonicity (antilegomenon); Luther's Preface questions it as derived from 2 Peter.

intros.author: "John" (1:1, 4, 9), exiled on the island of Patmos. Early tradition (Justin Martyr, Irenaeus) identifies him as the apostle John. Dionysius of Alexandria (3rd century) argued from style that it was a different John, and many modern scholars agree.
intros.date: Traditional and majority view: c. AD 95, under Domitian (Irenaeus). Some argue for c. AD 68–69, under or shortly after Nero, before the destruction of the temple.
intros.audience: The seven churches of the Roman province of Asia (Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea), and through them the whole Church.
intros.setting: Christians in Asia faced pressure to participate in the imperial cult and trade-guild idolatry, conflict with local synagogues, false teachers, complacency, and the threat of persecution.
intros.empires: The Roman Empire, symbolized (in the view of most interpreters) by the beast and by "Babylon the great," the city on seven hills (17:9). The imperial cult was especially strong in Asia Minor. The Lutheran tradition has also read the visions as describing the whole course of Church history until Christ's return.
intros.genre: Apocalyptic prophecy within a letter frame, rich in Old Testament imagery (especially from Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah, Isaiah) and in symbolic numbers (seven, twelve, 666, 144,000, 1,000).
intros.purpose: To reveal Jesus Christ, the Lamb who was slain and reigns, and to encourage the persecuted Church to remain faithful, knowing that God will judge evil and make all things new.
intros.themes: The sovereignty of God on His throne; the slain and victorious Lamb; worship in heaven; the conflict between Christ and Satan, the beast and the false prophet; the judgments (seals, trumpets, bowls); the faithful witness of the saints; the fall of Babylon; the marriage supper of the Lamb; the new heaven, new earth and new Jerusalem; "Even so, come, Lord Jesus" (22:20).
outline: 12–14 The woman, the dragon, and the beasts
17–19 The fall of Babylon; the Rider on the white horse
20 The thousand years and the final judgment
21–22 New heaven, new earth, new Jerusalem
intros.christ: Christ is "Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending" (1:8; 22:13), "the Lion of the tribe of Juda" who is the Lamb "as it had been slain" (5:5–6), who "loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood" (1:5), "KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS" (19:16), and the Bridegroom of the Church.
debated: Authorship — Traditional: the apostle John (Justin Martyr, Irenaeus). Main critical view: a different John (a Christian prophet), as Dionysius of Alexandria argued from the style.
Date — Traditional (Irenaeus): late in Domitian's reign, c. AD 95; this is also the majority modern view. Alternative: under or shortly after Nero, c. AD 68.

Interpretive approach — preterist (fulfilled mainly in the 1st century), historicist (a prophecy of Church history; the dominant Lutheran and Reformation view, as in Luther's 1530 Preface), futurist (mostly yet future), idealist (timeless symbols of the conflict between good and evil); many combine approaches.

The millennium (20:1–6) — amillennial (the thousand years as the present age of Christ's reign; the confessional Lutheran view, which rejects chiliasm, Augsburg Confession XVII), premillennial, and postmillennial views.
Canonicity — Revelation was disputed in the early Eastern church, and Luther's 1522 Preface expressed doubts about it, which he moderated in 1530.
