empires.name: Egypt
empires.period: c. 3000 BC onward; native pharaohs until the Persian conquest (525 BC), then Macedonian Ptolemies until Rome took Egypt (30 BC); New Kingdom c. 1550–1070 BC
empires.capital: Memphis, Thebes; later Sais, Tanis, and (under the Ptolemies) Alexandria
empires.summary: The Nile valley kingdom was the oldest great power of the biblical world. Its wealth rested on the annual flood of the Nile, which made Egypt the breadbasket that drew Abraham, Jacob's sons, and later the holy family in times of need. Pharaoh was regarded as a divine king, and Egyptian religion honored a large pantheon including Ra (the sun), Osiris, Isis, Horus, and the Nile and Apis bull cults.
empires.bible: Abraham sojourns in Egypt (Gen 12); Joseph rises to power and Israel settles in Goshen (Gen 37–50); the oppression and Exodus (Exod 1–15), which Scripture presents as the LORD's judgment "against all the gods of Egypt" (Exod 12:12); Solomon's marriage alliance (1 Kgs 3:1); Shishak's invasion of Judah (1 Kgs 14:25–26); Judah's repeated temptation to trust Egypt against Assyria and Babylon, condemned by Isaiah and Jeremiah (Isa 30–31; Jer 42–44); Pharaoh Necho kills Josiah at Megiddo (2 Kgs 23:29); the holy family's flight (Matt 2:13–15, fulfilling Hos 11:1).
empires.dating: The date of the Exodus is debated: traditional/early date c. 1446 BC (from 1 Kgs 6:1) vs. a 13th-century date under Ramesses II favored by many archaeologists. Both views are held by scholars who accept the Exodus as historical.
empires.legacy: Egypt is the Bible's chief picture of bondage, and the Exodus becomes the template for redemption, fulfilled in Christ, our Passover (1 Cor 5:7).

empires.name: Assyria
empires.capital: Assur, Calah (Nimrud), Dur-Sharrukin, and finally Nineveh
empires.summary: From northern Mesopotamia on the upper Tigris, Assyria built the first truly imperial state of the Near East, with a professional army, siege warfare, a network of provinces, and the policy of mass deportation of conquered peoples. Its royal inscriptions and palace reliefs boast of terror as a tool of rule.
empires.kings: Shalmaneser III (Jehu shown paying tribute on the Black Obelisk); Tiglath-pileser III (called Pul, 2 Kgs 15:19); Shalmaneser V and Sargon II (fall of Samaria, 722 BC); Sennacherib (siege of Jerusalem, 701 BC; his annals say he shut Hezekiah up "like a bird in a cage" but do not claim the city's capture); Esarhaddon; Ashurbanipal.
empires.bible: Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel and resettled Samaria with foreigners (2 Kgs 17), the origin of later Samaritan tensions. Isaiah calls Assyria "the rod of mine anger" (Isa 10:5) yet announces its judgment; Jerusalem was delivered in Hezekiah's day (2 Kgs 18–19; Isa 36–37). Jonah preached in Nineveh; Nahum and Zephaniah foretold its fall.
empires.fall: Nineveh fell to a coalition of Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC; the last Assyrian resistance ended at Harran and Carchemish (609–605 BC).
empires.legacy: Assyria shows God ruling even over pagan empires, using them and then judging their pride.

empires.name: Babylon
empires.summary: Under Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar II (605–562 BC), Babylon inherited Assyria's empire. Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt the city magnificently, with the Ishtar Gate, Processional Way, and great temple of Marduk (Esagila) with its ziggurat. Babylonian religion centered on Marduk (Bel) and Nabu (Nebo).
empires.bible: Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish (605 BC; Jer 46:2), took captives including Daniel (Dan 1), deported Jehoiachin and Ezekiel (597 BC), and destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon's temple (586 BC; 2 Kgs 25; Jer 52; Lamentations). Jeremiah foretold seventy years of servitude (Jer 25:11–12; 29:10). Habakkuk wrestles with God's use of the Chaldeans. The book of Daniel portrays Nebuchadnezzar humbled and Belshazzar's last feast.
empires.history: Babylonian records confirm Jehoiachin received rations in Babylon (cf. 2 Kgs 25:27–30). Belshazzar, once doubted by critics, is attested as son and co-regent of the last king, Nabonidus, which fits his offer to make Daniel "third ruler" (Dan 5:16).
empires.fall: Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC, largely without a battle.
empires.legacy: In later Scripture "Babylon" becomes a symbol of the proud world system opposed to God (Rev 17–18).

empires.name: Persia
empires.summary: Cyrus the Great united the Medes and Persians and built the largest empire the world had yet seen, stretching from the Aegean to India. Persian policy allowed subject peoples to keep their customs and temples, organized the empire into satrapies, and built a royal road and postal system. The Persian kings were generally devotees of Ahura Mazda.
empires.kings: Cyrus II (559–530); Cambyses; Darius I (522–486; temple completed 516/515 BC); Xerxes I, the Ahasuerus of Esther (486–465); Artaxerxes I (465–424; Ezra and Nehemiah).
empires.bible: Isaiah names Cyrus as the LORD's "anointed" shepherd (Isa 44:28–45:1). Cyrus's decree permitted the return of the exiles (Ezra 1; 2 Chr 36:22–23), a policy echoed on the Cyrus Cylinder. Haggai and Zechariah urged rebuilding the temple under Darius. Esther is set at the court in Susa; Ezra and Nehemiah lead later returns and rebuild the walls.
empires.fall: Alexander the Great defeated Darius III (333–331 BC).
empires.legacy: The Persian period shaped the post-exilic community: the second temple, the renewed reading of the Law, and the growth of Aramaic as a common language.

empires.name: Greece, the Ptolemies and the Seleucids
empires.period: Alexander 336–323 BC; Ptolemaic Egypt 323–30 BC; Seleucid Syria 312–63 BC
empires.summary: Alexander of Macedon conquered Persia and spread Greek language and culture (Hellenism) as far as India. After his early death his generals divided the empire. Judea was ruled first by the Ptolemies of Egypt (to c. 200 BC), then by the Seleucids of Syria. Koine Greek became the common tongue of the eastern Mediterranean, the language of the Septuagint and the New Testament.
empires.events: In Alexandria the Hebrew Scriptures were translated into Greek (the Septuagint, from the 3rd century BC). The Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175–164 BC) banned Jewish worship and desecrated the temple (167 BC), provoking the Maccabean revolt; the temple was rededicated in 164 BC (the feast of Dedication, John 10:22). The Hasmonean dynasty then ruled an independent Judea until Rome arrived.
empires.bible: These events fall between the Testaments. Traditional interpreters see them foretold in Daniel 8 and 11 (the "rough goat," the divided kingdom, the king of the north and south, and the "abomination that maketh desolate"); critical scholars generally date Daniel's final form to the Maccabean crisis (c. 165 BC). See the Daniel introduction for both views.
empires.legacy: Greek culture and language prepared the way for the spread of the Gospel across the Mediterranean world.

empires.name: Rome
empires.period: Republic to 27 BC; Empire from Augustus (27 BC–AD 14) onward
empires.summary: Rome expanded from Italy to master the whole Mediterranean. Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC. Rome ruled Judea through client kings (Herod the Great, 37–4 BC; his sons Archelaus, Antipas, Philip; Agrippa I and II) and prefects or procurators (including Pontius Pilate, AD 26–36; Felix; Festus). The Pax Romana, Roman roads, and Roman citizenship shaped the setting of the New Testament.
empires.emperors: Augustus (Luke 2:1); Tiberius (Luke 3:1); Caligula; Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2); Nero, to whom Paul appealed and under whom Peter and Paul are traditionally said to have been martyred; Vespasian and Titus, who destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70; Domitian, under whom many date Revelation.
empires.bible: Jesus was born under Augustus and crucified under Pontius Pilate. Paul's Roman citizenship protected him (Acts 16:37; 22:25–29) and brought him to Rome (Acts 25:11; 28). Romans 13 teaches obedience to governing authority; Revelation portrays a persecuting world power in the image of a beast and "Babylon."
empires.legacy: Christ's kingdom, though it did not come with Roman swords, spread through the very roads and peace of the empire, until the faith persecuted by Rome outlasted it.
